\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Validation-selected predictive comparison'', under ``Paired temporal-block inference'':}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
The original manuscript contained no paired temporal-block uncertainty analysis. The following subsection has been added.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\par\noindent\textbf{Paired temporal-block inference}\par
{\color{blue}For every task and timestamp, we first average squared error over each method's declared evaluation seeds and then subtract the comparator's value from the TL-QLDMR value; negative differences favor TL-QLDMR. The timestamps are partitioned into non-overlapping Monday--Sunday seven-calendar-day blocks. We use 10,000 whole-block bootstrap resamples for a percentile 95\% interval and 99,999 two-sided paired block sign flips with a plus-one correction. Holm adjustment is applied in two separate families of 30 tests, one for the six primary tasks and one for the six secondary tasks, with five TL-QLDMR comparisons per task. The bootstrap treats block effects as approximately independent and exchangeable, while the sign-flip test additionally requires approximate sign symmetry under the null.}

{\color{blue}As a complementary scope-level summary, all 15 method pairs are compared using 99,999 two-sided seven-day block swaps of the exact site-equal capacity-normalized seed-mean macro-RMSE endpoint, with Holm adjustment applied separately within each scope. When a pair contains deterministic HistGBR, its single timewise error curve is compared with each kernel seed curve under the same block swaps; this preserves the declared seed-mean endpoint and does not treat the repeated deterministic curve as independent replication. The conservative first tier contains the empirical endpoint winner and every method whose inferiority to that winner is not established by the predeclared strict adjusted-$p<0.05$ exclusion rule. Membership indicates non-rejection of inferiority under this block procedure; it is not evidence of equivalence, does not establish superiority, and is not a formal model-confidence set.}

{\color{blue}The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. The Holm-significant scope-level TL-QLDMR relations were: In the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 4.178 percentage points higher than HistGBR; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$). In the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 0.511 percentage points higher than No variance; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). These tests concern the prespecified macro endpoint; empirical ordering by itself is not a significance claim.}

{\color{blue}The Holm-significant TL-QLDMR comparisons were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.539, -0.139]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $204.912$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[71.894, 425.012]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.012$). Farm~3 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $71.623$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[35.870, 114.080]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.011$). Farm~1 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $214.556$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[91.628, 413.791]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.001$). Farm~6 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $16.917$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[9.148, 27.398]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). All other predeclared TL-QLDMR comparisons were not significant after adjustment; this absence of rejection is not evidence of equal performance.}

{\color{blue}Table~30 retains all task-level TL-QLDMR comparisons, including nonsignificant and adverse effects. The test period is reused and the number of temporal blocks is limited, so these paired results are interpreted conservatively.}
\end{quote}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Conclusion'', the evidence-summary paragraph:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
Experimental results show that TL-QLDMR delivers consistent gains in both deterministic and interval forecasting on the most challenging target farm. For point prediction, it achieves the best RMSE (7.478) and $R^2$ (0.9557). For 95\% interval prediction, it attains PICP $=0.959$ together with the best CWC (0.268), indicating a favorable reliability-sharpness trade-off. Under injected noise, TL-QLDMR remains the strongest model across reported point and interval metrics. In addition, the Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver provides practical scalability, completing the full uncapped training set ($N=69{,}737$) in 5.021 seconds, whereas CVXOPT, Torch-GD, and batch SGD do not remain computationally viable at the same scale.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The implementation passes deterministic objective, gradient, and primal--dual consistency checks. In the primary within-site scope, histogram gradient boosting had the lowest observed site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties; it ranked 3rd of six and was excluded from the conservative first tier. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, histogram gradient boosting had the lowest observed site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties; it ranked 5th of six and was retained in the conservative first tier. The first-tier statements are non-rejections of inferiority to each empirical endpoint winner and do not establish equivalence, equal performance, or superiority. Among 60 predeclared task-level comparisons, 1 Holm-adjusted finding favored TL-QLDMR and 4 favored a comparator; non-rejection for the remaining comparisons does not establish equal performance. In the conditional matched-removal analysis for the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR recorded 18.090\% and ranked 2nd of four by macro RMSE, with the lowest mean task rank (2.00); the lowest observed matched endpoint was the no-variance variant at 17.870\%. In the conditional matched-removal analysis for the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR recorded 17.694\% and ranked 2nd of four by macro RMSE, with the lowest mean task rank (2.17); the lowest observed matched endpoint was the no-variance variant at 17.671\%. Across 36 matched task-level contrasts, 2 Holm-adjusted effects favored TL-QLDMR and 0 favored a removal variant. These effects are conditional on the TL-QLDMR-selected settings; the variants were not independently retuned, and non-rejection does not establish equivalence. The separate Farm~6 nine-quantile and earlier calibration studies remain legacy exploratory sensitivity analyses and are not part of the formal evidence chain. Taken together, the formal results provide a scope- and task-dependent assessment of TL-QLDMR rather than evidence of universal superiority. Because the public Q3--Q4 test period had been examined before the frozen protocol was designed, the comparison is test-locked evidence on a reused period and does not provide independent external confirmation.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE conclusion_evidence

% -------------Reviewer 1, Concern 8--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 1, Concern 8}}}
\emph{The temporal validation strategy is not sufficiently explicit for a forecasting problem. The manuscript should clarify whether the train/validation/test split is strictly chronological; if random splitting was used anywhere, it may leak future information and overstate performance in a time-series setting.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We replaced the random-window description with a strictly chronological target-time protocol. Models are fitted only on 2019 observations; Q1 2020 is used only by the frozen formal model-selection procedure, Q2 supplies interval-calibration labels, and Q3--Q4 supplies evaluation labels. The formal workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after both its selection and analysis specifications are locked, while the matched point analysis uses no Q2 label and locks its configurations and analysis specification before its Q3--Q4 evaluation. Each forecast uses the preceding 24 consecutive 15-minute observations to predict the next 15-minute target. Adjacent windows across a boundary may share already observed history, as in rolling forecasting, but every target timestamp belongs to one period only. No Q1, Q2, or Q3--Q4 label enters the 2019 fit; no Q2 or Q3--Q4 label enters Q1 selection; and no Q3--Q4 label enters fixed Q2 calibration. Past-only rolling calibration is identified separately because it may use only outcomes revealed strictly before the current forecast and appends the current outcome only after issuing that forecast. Randomness is confined to fitting-label acquisition and landmark seeds, not the calendar partition.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We replaced the former random-split setup and added a complete chronological split, window-construction, and label-flow description in the experimental protocol.

% BEGIN VERIFIED CHANGE experimental_setup
\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Validation-selected predictive comparison'', near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
The hyperparameters of TL-QLDMR are selected by validation-based tuning within each experiment. The searched ranges are logarithmic grids for $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$ from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{6}$, $C_S \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.2\}$, $C_T \in \{50, 300, 1000\}$, and kernel bandwidth $\gamma \in \{2^{-6}, \ldots, 2^{6}\}$. The Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver is tuned over landmark size $m \in [800, 1500]$, learning rate in $\{0.005, 0.01\}$, and training epochs in $[48, 80]$, with mini-batch size fixed at 256. All experiments are implemented in Python and executed on a GPU server equipped with eight NVIDIA Tesla V100-SXM2-32GB GPUs (32\,GB memory per GPU), using NVIDIA driver version 550.54.15 and CUDA 12.4. All random splits use a fixed seed for reproducibility.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\par\noindent\textbf{Validation-selected predictive comparison}\par
{\color{blue}We compare TL-QLDMR, its no-variance and no-discrepancy variants, pooled weighted support vector quantile regression (SVQR), target-only SVQR, and histogram gradient boosting with quantile loss (HistGBR). The six within-site normal-to-extreme tasks form the primary scope, and the six leave-one-farm-out tasks form a secondary transfer-stress scope. Every site and method is retained in its prespecified scope. Within each primary task, the source observations are normal-domain windows from the target farm; within each secondary task, normal-domain source observations come from the other five farms.}

{\color{blue}Each task uses exactly 128 extreme-domain target fitting labels selected deterministically from 2019. The cells are training month crossed with mutually exclusive cold, hot, and high-wind/cut-out categories, assigned in that priority order from target-time meteorological covariates within the fitting period only; power values are not used in acquisition. Each nonempty cell first receives one observation; the remaining labels are allocated by the largest-remainder rule in proportion to the cells' remaining capacities, and observations within a cell are chosen near equally spaced clock-time targets. A primary task uses at most 7,500 normal-domain source windows from the same farm, deterministically thinned in chronological order, whereas a secondary task uses at most 1,500 normal-domain source windows from each of the other five farms. The 128 labels are the model-fitting budget rather than the total target supervision. For Farms~1--6, the additional target-domain Q1 selection counts are 169, 617, 2,410, 212, 134, and 177, and the Q2 calibration counts are 305, 102, 862, 319, 362, and 225, respectively.}

{\color{blue}The formal-comparison input at each forecast contains four wind-speed measurements, sine and cosine encodings of four wind-direction measurements, temperature, atmospheric pressure, and relative humidity at each of the 24 strictly preceding 15-minute observations, giving 360 flattened meteorological inputs. Past power and future meteorological values are excluded. Power labels are divided by their farm-specific nominal capacity before fit-only label standardization and are mapped back to the target farm's MW scale for evaluation. Missing-value imputation and feature and label standardization are fitted only on the 2019 model-fitting rows. For pooled models, the source and target domains each contribute one half of the preprocessing weight; target-only preprocessing uses only its target fitting rows. Nystr\"om landmarks are constructed without labels from fitting inputs. A pooled landmark pool contains at most 2,000 source and 2,000 target rows and assigns total K-means weight one half to each domain; target-only construction uses only target fitting rows. K-means is used when the requested rank is smaller than the pool, while all pool rows are retained when the requested rank equals the pool size; any resulting effective-rank cap is recorded.}

{\color{blue}For each task--method pair, the frozen search rule issues 54 effective Q1 configuration queries through three predeclared sequential stages of 18 new queries: a base search, a middle active-regularizer search or method-equivalent refinement, and a local joint refinement. The middle stage either varies the active regularizer coefficients while retaining the base incumbent's other coordinates or applies a method-equivalent deterministic refinement around that incumbent; the joint stage is generated locally around the incumbent retained after the middle stage. Within a task--method pair, the 18 effective configurations in each stage are distinct from one another and from every earlier-stage query, giving 54 distinct effective queries across the three stages. Kernel candidates are scored by the mean target-Q1 RMSE of the $\tau=0.5$ fit across seeds 0, 1, and 2, whereas deterministic HistGBR is fitted once at seed 0 per query. The pooled kernel searches include requested Nystr\"om ranks 128, 256, and 512, and target-only SVQR uses ranks 32, 64, and 128. Inactive hyperparameter coordinates are ignored when effective-query uniqueness is checked. Equal query counts provide a common configuration-query budget; they do not imply equal model capacity, numbers of solver attempts, wall-clock cost, or exhaustive optimization.}

{\color{blue}Candidate generation, model fitting, preprocessing, landmark construction, and Q1 scoring are completed before the immutable selection lock is created, and the analysis specification is separately frozen before any formal-comparison Q3--Q4 output is read. Each locked configuration is refitted on the unchanged 2019 fitting rows; Q1 labels are not added to the fit. Q2 is reserved for interval calibration, and the formal workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after the selection and analysis locks and then evaluates it under the locked settings. Kernel settings use landmark seeds 0, 1, and 2, and deterministic HistGBR uses seed 0. No task, method, seed, or configuration is selected from Q2 or Q3--Q4 performance. Because the public-data test period had already been examined in earlier work, this design provides test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation.}

{\color{blue}Every kernel fit is first attempted for at most 3,000 ADMM iterations. The numerical certificate is checked every 25 iterations and requires $P-D\leq 10^{-7}+10^{-3}\max\{1,|P|,|D|\}$. If the first attempt misses this condition, a second attempt is warm-started from its returned best-primal $(\boldsymbol{w},b)$ incumbent, with freshly initialized split and dual states, and is allowed at most 12,000 additional ADMM iterations; the data, feature map, objective, and hyperparameters remain unchanged. The candidate remains in the audit record but is ineligible for selection if any required selection seed still misses the certificate. Under the original execution rule, a locked main-study or matched-ablation fit that still missed the certificate produced no retained result. This is a numerical primal--dual-gap certificate for the chosen fixed-feature objective, not an interval-arithmetic proof, a certificate of Nystr\"om approximation error, or a predictive-generalization guarantee.}

{\color{blue}One locked main-study fit exhausted these two attempts with a relative gap of 0.0010217, compared with the unchanged 0.001 tolerance. Before its Q3--Q4 predictive scores were inspected, we froze a performance-blind solver amendment that committed the hashes of all then-existing completion artifacts and the already frozen analysis specifications. For an otherwise exact locked main or matched fit with no completed result, the amendment permitted one further warm restart, from the same best-primal incumbent and fresh split and dual states, for at most 96,000 iterations under the same objective, data, feature map, hyperparameters, and certificate tolerance. No completed result could be replaced. The single triggering main-study fit then met the unchanged certificate; no matched-ablation fit required the amendment. Selection, calibration, prediction, and analysis rules were unchanged, and the original failed record, model, amendment lock, and completion sidecars are retained in the reproducibility package.}
\end{quote}

% -------------Reviewer 1, Concern 9--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 1, Concern 9}}}
\emph{The scalability claim is positive, but the computational analysis is incomplete. The Nystr\"om-SGD solver should be evaluated more thoroughly across a wider range of landmark sizes and data scales, with an explicit accuracy-runtime trade-off curve, because the current runtime advantage alone does not show whether approximation error becomes significant.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We now separate three questions: exact-kernel optimization, optimization of a fixed Nystr\"om feature problem, and predictive approximation as rank changes. The formal v2 comparison uses a convex fixed-feature ADMM objective. Every kernel validation fit is first checked every 25 iterations against absolute tolerance $10^{-7}$ and relative tolerance $10^{-3}$ for at most 3,000 iterations. A fit that misses the certificate is retried once from the returned best-primal $(\boldsymbol{w},b)$ incumbent using a fresh ADMM split and dual state, with the data, features, objective, and hyperparameters unchanged, for at most 12,000 additional iterations. A candidate remains in the audit trail but is ineligible if any required selection seed still misses the certificate. The audited Q1 search issued 3,888 distinct within-task--method configuration queries (54 per pair) and 10,368 fit records; 3,455 queried candidates were eligible under the frozen selection rule. Among 9,720 kernel seed fits, 1,214 still missed the fixed-feature primal--dual-gap certificate after the predeclared retry and therefore made their candidate ineligible; 8,506 kernel seed fits met the certificate. Across kernel and HistGBR fits, the records contain 12,691 solver attempts and 32,207,875 reported iterations. Summed per-fit recorded time was 50.70 h. This sum is descriptive because tasks ran in parallel; it is neither elapsed wall-clock time nor inference latency. The certificate applies only to the chosen fixed-feature objective and does not certify Nyström approximation error or predictive generalization. One locked main-study fit ended the original attempts with relative gap 0.0010217 against the unchanged 0.001 tolerance. Before that fit's predictive scores were inspected, a performance-blind amendment hash-committed all then-existing completion artifacts (10 main and 5 matched result records, without parsing their metrics) and the then-existing analysis files. It permitted only an otherwise identical locked fit with no completed result to receive one additional warm restart of at most 96,000 iterations. The objective, data, feature map, configuration, seed, quantile, tolerances, prediction procedure, and analysis rules were unchanged, and no completed result could be replaced. The single triggering main-study fit then met the unchanged certificate; no matched-ablation fit used the amendment. This is numerical accounting for the fixed-feature optimization problem, not a bound on Nystr\"om approximation error, prediction error, or deployment latency. This certificate concerns numerical optimization of the chosen fixed-feature objective; it does not bound Nystr\"om approximation error or predictive generalization.

The earlier common-setting study retains accuracy--runtime curves over multiple landmark counts and source-data scales as descriptive sensitivity evidence. Those measurements include the stated fitting components and are not used to claim a deployment latency or a method speed ranking. The manuscript therefore presents an empirical rank/data-scale trade-off and a separately audited fixed-feature optimization certificate, without claiming that runtime alone establishes negligible approximation error or operational readiness.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised, added, and removed the relevant text in Sections ``Proposed Method'' and ``Experiments''. The exact original wording and revised text are reproduced below at each approximate location.

Its implementation and computational costs are described below; the approximate objective is not identified with the exact kernel objective.}
\end{quote}

% BEGIN VERIFIED CHANGE feature_map
\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Proposed Method'', subsection ``Scalable Optimization via Nystr\"{o}m Approximation'', near the revised passage:}\par

\begingroup\ResponseOriginalSafeOn\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
To keep the scalable solver consistent with the exact kernelized problem in Eq. (\ref{eq:kernel_primal}), we replace the implicit RKHS mapping $\phi(\boldsymbol{x})$ with an explicit $m$-dimensional Nystr\"{o}m feature map. We select $m$ landmark points $Z = \{z_1, \ldots, z_m\}$ from the combined training set $D = D_S \cup D_T$ via K-Means clustering \citep{zhang2010clustered}. Let $\boldsymbol{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$ denote the kernel matrix among landmarks, where $W_{ij} = k(z_i, z_j)$. The explicit feature mapping $\psi: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:nystrom_feature}
\psi(\boldsymbol{x}) = \boldsymbol{W}^{-1/2} [k(\boldsymbol{x}, z_1), \ldots, k(\boldsymbol{x}, z_m)]^T,
\end{equation}
where $\boldsymbol{W}^{-1/2}$ is computed via eigendecomposition, satisfying $k(\boldsymbol{x}_i, \boldsymbol{x}_j) \approx \psi(\boldsymbol{x}_i)^T \psi(\boldsymbol{x}_j)$.
\end{quote}
\endgroup\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}For a fixed RBF bandwidth, every landmark is selected without labels from model-fitting inputs only. The fixed-setting Adam sensitivity track retains its original pool of at most 2,000 source fitting inputs, while a target-only fit uses its target fitting inputs. In the formal validation-selected comparison, imputation, feature standardization, and capacity-normalized label standardization are fitted with row weights totaling 0.5 over the source rows and 0.5 over the target rows; a target-only fit uses equal weights over its target fitting rows. For each pooled fit, the landmark pool draws at most 2,000 fitting rows from each domain and assigns the source and target subsets total K-means weights of 0.5 each, whereas target-only landmark construction uses only target fitting rows with equal row weights. The requested ranks are 128, 256, and 512 for pooled kernel methods and 32, 64, and 128 for TargetSVQR. If a pool exceeds the requested rank, K-means selects that many centers using the stated domain weights where applicable \citep{zhang2010clustered}; otherwise all pool inputs are retained without clustering. In particular, at requested rank 128, TargetSVQR retains all 128 target fitting inputs as landmarks and does not run K-means. Thus $m$ denotes the effective number of landmarks and is transparently capped by the pool size. The calling experiment fixes the random state before subset selection, and the validation runner records that seed and the selected landmarks, which remain fixed during optimization. Let $\boldsymbol{W}$ be their Gram matrix and $\boldsymbol{k}_Z(\boldsymbol{x})=[k(\boldsymbol{x},z_1),\ldots,k(\boldsymbol{x},z_m)]^T$. A stabilized feature map is}
\begin{equation}
{\color{blue}\psi(\boldsymbol{x})=(\boldsymbol{W}+\varepsilon\boldsymbol{I})^{-1/2}\boldsymbol{k}_Z(\boldsymbol{x}),\qquad \varepsilon=10^{-6}.}
\end{equation}
{\color{blue}The symmetric inverse square root is formed by SVD or symmetric eigendecomposition. The resulting fixed kernel approximation is $\widetilde{k}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{x}_{*})=\psi(\boldsymbol{x})^T\psi(\boldsymbol{x}_{*})$; finite landmark size and stabilization both affect this approximation. No approximation-error bound is assumed.}
\end{quote}

The approximate objective is jointly convex and is strongly convex in $\boldsymbol{w}$ for fixed $b$, but the unregularized intercept precludes a claim of joint strong convexity. The common-setting study uses Adam with a fixed learning rate and a finite number of epochs. Convexity alone does not establish convergence or an $O(1/T)$ rate for this implementation; no such rate is asserted. Likewise, no bound relating its solution to the exact kernel optimum is asserted. Landmark size, stabilization, and optimization accuracy must be assessed empirically.}
\end{quote}

The full, no-variance, no-discrepancy, and target-only variants use seeds 0, 1, and 2. These are algorithmic repeats on a shared test period, not independent datasets or confidence intervals.}

{\color{blue}Point prediction uses $\tau=0.5$. Interval fits use $\tau_L=0.025$ and $\tau_U=0.975$. Define ordered endpoints $\ell(x)=\min\{f_{\tau_L}(x),f_{\tau_U}(x)\}$ and $u(x)=\max\{f_{\tau_L}(x),f_{\tau_U}(x)\}$. Calibration scores are $s_i=\max\{\ell(x_i)-y_i,y_i-u(x_i),0\}$. With $\alpha=0.05$, set $k=\lceil(n_{\rm cal}+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$, $q=s_{(k)}$, and report $[\ell(x)-q,u(x)+q]$. A finite interval requires $k\le n_{\rm cal}$. On Farm~6, $n_{\rm cal}=225$ and $k=215$. This formula defines the fixed Q2 expansion, to which no Q3--Q4 label contributes. The separately reported past-only rolling expansion may use only Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed before each forecast; it never uses the current or a future outcome. These are empirical temporal evaluations without an exchangeability or conditional-coverage guarantee \citep{romano2019cqr}.}

{\color{blue}Each branch saves source/target fitting identifiers, preprocessing statistics, landmarks, model coefficients, calibration scores, and individual test predictions. Code and workbook hashes accompany the fixed protocol. Reported fitting time includes landmark selection, feature construction, regularizer construction, and Adam, but excludes workbook loading, preprocessing, prediction, and post-fit objective diagnostics. Timings are wall-clock measurements from a shared compute host. Seed ranges throughout these analyses describe algorithmic variation rather than confidence intervals; fitting times do not represent inference or deployment latency.}
\end{quote}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Proposed Method'', subsection ``Optimization accuracy for fixed features'', near the added passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
The original manuscript contains no corresponding fixed-feature ADMM accuracy analysis.

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\par\noindent\textbf{Optimization accuracy for fixed features}\par
{\color{blue}To monitor optimization accuracy for each fixed-feature fit, we also solve Eq.~(20) by the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) \citep{boyd2011admm}. Let $\boldsymbol{Z}=[\boldsymbol{\Psi}_S^T,\boldsymbol{\Psi}_T^T]^T$ and introduce residuals $\boldsymbol{e}=\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{Z}\boldsymbol{w}-b\mathbf1$. The quadratic weight/intercept update eliminates the unregularized intercept by centering $\boldsymbol{Z}$, then solves an $m\times m$ system with matrix $\boldsymbol{R}+\rho\boldsymbol{Z}_c^T\boldsymbol{Z}_c$. The residual update is elementwise asymmetric soft thresholding, with positive and negative thresholds $C_i\tau/\rho$ and $C_i(1-\tau)/\rho$. The penalty parameter $\rho$ is adjusted using training residuals only.}

{\color{blue}A feasible dual vector supplies a numerical lower bound on the fixed-feature optimum. With the same label-only constant omitted as in Eq.~(20), the dual is}
\begin{equation}
{\color{blue}\begin{aligned}
\max_{\boldsymbol{v}}\quad D(\boldsymbol{v})
&=\boldsymbol{y}^T\boldsymbol{v}-\frac12(\boldsymbol{c}+\boldsymbol{Z}^T\boldsymbol{v})^T
\boldsymbol{R}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{c}+\boldsymbol{Z}^T\boldsymbol{v}),\\
\text{s.t.}\quad \mathbf1^T\boldsymbol{v}&=0,\qquad C_i(\tau-1)\le v_i\le C_i\tau.
\end{aligned}}
\end{equation}
{\color{blue}This follows by minimizing the Lagrangian over $\boldsymbol{w}$ and $b$ and applying the conjugate of the weighted pinball loss. Projecting the ADMM multiplier onto the box and zero-sum constraints gives a feasible dual iterate. For the best retained primal and dual values, $P-D$ bounds training suboptimality up to numerical feasibility error. The common numerical certificate is $P-D\le10^{-7}+10^{-3}\max\{1,|P|,|D|\}$, checked every 25 iterations. In the formal validation-selected comparison, every kernel fit is first attempted with a cap of 3,000 ADMM iterations. If that attempt misses the certificate, one predeclared retry starts a fresh ADMM state initialized only from the returned best-primal $(\boldsymbol{w},b)$ incumbent; no split residual or dual state is retained, and the retry has its own cap of 12,000 iterations. The fitting rows, fixed feature map, objective, hyperparameters, seed, quantile, tolerances, and check frequency remain unchanged. A validation candidate remains in the audit record but is ineligible for selection if any required selection seed remains uncertified after the retry. The locked point-and-interval evaluation accepts each kernel fit at $\tau\in\{0.5,0.025,0.975\}$ only after the same certificate is met, and the matched point ablation applies the same requirement at $\tau=0.5$; an uncertified locked fit stops the corresponding workflow rather than being scored. HistGBR is outside this fixed-feature primal--dual certificate. The absolute gap is unchanged by the omitted label-only constant; the relative normalization refers specifically to the displayed objective. Every kernel run retains its gap, feasibility residuals, attempt summaries, and final stopping status. This certificate concerns numerical optimization of the stated fixed-feature training objective; it does not certify equivalence to the exact-kernel problem, Nystr\"{o}m approximation error, or predictive generalization.}

{\color{blue}After constructing $\boldsymbol{Z}_c^T\boldsymbol{Z}_c$, each ADMM iteration costs $O(Nm+m^2)$; a change of $\rho$ requires another $O(m^3)$ factorization. Diagnostic checks additionally evaluate the training objective and feasible dual bound, optimize the intercept by a weighted-quantile sort, and project the dual vector. Their cost is $O(Nm+m^2+N\log N)$ with a fixed cap on the scalar projection iterations. Small problems at three quantiles, including rank-deficient features and unequal or zero sample weights, are checked against an independently formulated primal quadratic program.}
\end{quote}

% -------------Reviewer 1, Concern 10--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 1, Concern 10}}}
\emph{The conclusions would be stronger if the manuscript tested robustness beyond injected noise on one farm. The paper should include ablations under multiple meteorological seasons, different extreme-event types, and possibly additional datasets, to show that the observed robustness is general rather than dataset-specific.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We removed the under-specified injected-noise experiment and broadened the predictive evidence to twelve complete tasks. The six within-site normal-to-extreme tasks form the primary scope, while six leave-one-farm-out tasks form a harder secondary transfer-stress scope. Every target farm, method, and prescribed seed is retained, and the two scopes are summarized separately by site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE and average task rank. In the primary within-site scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 3rd of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 5th of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. The Holm-significant scope-level TL-QLDMR relations were: In the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 4.178 percentage points higher than HistGBR; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$). In the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 0.511 percentage points higher than No variance; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). These tests concern the prespecified macro endpoint; empirical ordering by itself is not a significance claim. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. The Holm-significant TL-QLDMR comparisons were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.539, -0.139]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $204.912$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[71.894, 425.012]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.012$). Farm~3 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $71.623$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[35.870, 114.080]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.011$). Farm~1 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $214.556$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[91.628, 413.791]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.001$). Farm~6 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $16.917$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[9.148, 27.398]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). All other predeclared TL-QLDMR comparisons were not significant after adjustment; this absence of rejection is not evidence of equal performance. This design tests whether the observed behavior persists across target sites and across a cross-site shift without selecting farms by held-out performance.

Seasonal composition, meteorological-tail type, scarcity, weighting, and objectively defined contiguous episodes remain separate descriptive sensitivity analyses. The episode rule uses the longest contiguous episode at each site, with earliest start as a tie-breaker, and does not use prediction error. These analyses still cover Q3--Q4 of one public six-farm dataset; tail membership is defined retrospectively from target-time weather, categories can overlap, and no independent storm labels or additional external dataset were introduced. The revised manuscript therefore reports broader multi-site robustness evidence while limiting generalization to the observed farms, periods, and shift constructions.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised, added, and removed the relevant text in the Abstract, Sections ``Experiments'' and ``Conclusion'', and Appendix ``Validation-selected comparison details''. The exact original wording and revised text are reproduced below at each approximate location.

% BEGIN VERIFIED CHANGE abstract
\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Abstract, near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
Accurate wind power forecasting under extreme events is critical for grid stability and renewable energy integration, yet remains a formidable challenge due to severe data scarcity and substantial distribution shifts between normal and extreme-event operating regimes. While kernel-based methods, particularly support vector regression and Large-margin Distribution Machine-based Regression (LDMR), have demonstrated strong performance in various regression tasks due to their theoretical guarantees and robustness on limited data, their application to extreme-event forecasting faces critical limitations: the i.i.d. assumption underlying standard kernel methods is fundamentally violated under cross-domain scenarios, and the symmetric variance minimization in LDMR implicitly encourages symmetric error distributions, which conflicts with the asymmetric nature of quantile-based interval prediction required for uncertainty quantification. To extend kernel-based regression to extreme-event forecasting, we propose Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR), which addresses these challenges through three synergistic innovations: (i) an asymmetric variance regularizer that preserves LDMR's distributional robustness while accommodating quantile-specific error asymmetry, (ii) a supervised transfer learning framework integrating maximum mean discrepancy for feature alignment and weighted pinball loss for label adaptation, enabling effective knowledge transfer from abundant normal-domain data to scarce extreme-event samples, and (iii) a scalable Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver reducing complexity from $O(N^3)$ to $O(T \cdot N \cdot m)$. Comprehensive experiments on six wind farms demonstrate that TL-QLDMR achieves competitive performance in both deterministic and probabilistic forecasting in the extreme-event domain, with superior reliability-sharpness trade-off and practical scalability, making it suitable for real-time applications where interpretability and theoretical guarantees are prioritized.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}Wind-power forecasting during meteorological extremes combines limited target labels with source--target distribution differences. We formulate the Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR) using symmetric centered source-residual variance, a projected predictive-mean discrepancy, and weighted pinball loss. A frozen chronological comparison uses 128 target fitting labels and separates six primary within-site tasks from six secondary leave-one-farm-out stress tasks. In the primary within-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 13.913\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 18.090\%, ranked 3rd of six, and was outside the conservative first tier. In the secondary cross-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 14.923\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 17.694\%, ranked 5th of six, and remained in the conservative first tier. First-tier membership is non-rejection of inferiority rather than equivalence or superiority. Of 60 Holm-adjusted task comparisons, 1 favored TL-QLDMR and 4 favored a comparator. With its settings held fixed, TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four in the primary matched scope and 2nd of four in the secondary matched scope; 2 Holm-adjusted removal effects favored TL-QLDMR and 0 favored a removal variant. TL-QLDMR had the lowest mean task rank in both matched scopes. The matched effects are conditional because the variants were not independently retuned. The public Q3--Q4 period had been examined previously, so these results are test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation and do not establish universal model superiority.}
\end{quote}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Conclusion'', near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
Experimental results show that TL-QLDMR delivers consistent gains in both deterministic and interval forecasting on the most challenging target farm. For point prediction, it achieves the best RMSE (7.478) and $R^2$ (0.9557). For 95\% interval prediction, it attains PICP $=0.959$ together with the best CWC (0.268), indicating a favorable reliability-sharpness trade-off. Under injected noise, TL-QLDMR remains the strongest model across reported point and interval metrics. In addition, the Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver provides practical scalability, completing the full uncapped training set ($N=69{,}737$) in 5.021 seconds, whereas CVXOPT, Torch-GD, and batch SGD do not remain computationally viable at the same scale.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The formal comparison uses a public six-farm dataset whose Q3--Q4 period had been examined before the frozen protocol was designed. Locking Q1 selection, the analysis specification, and the matched configurations before evaluation prevents further test-guided adaptation, but it does not turn the reused period into independent confirmation. The 128 target labels describe the fitting budget rather than total supervision because Q1 selection and Q2 calibration labels are additional; past-only rolling calibration further uses outcomes revealed before the current forecast. Equal configuration-query counts do not equalize model capacity, solver attempts, or wall-clock cost, algorithmic seed ranges are not confidence intervals, first-tier membership establishes non-rejection rather than equivalence, and matched removal effects are conditional on the TL-QLDMR-selected configuration. Chronological ordering does not remove serial dependence or establish conformal coverage guarantees. Meteorological-tail membership is defined retrospectively from target-time weather, with overlapping sample categories rather than independently tracked storms or ramp events. The numerical certificate applies only to each fixed-feature training objective, while Nystr\"{o}m approximation error, independent-farm generalization, longer forecast horizons, and deployment latency remain unestablished. The separate Farm~6 nine-quantile analysis is legacy exploratory evidence whose original archive did not freeze every current loader, sampler, or chronological-reference dependency.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\small
A critical prerequisite for evaluating transfer learning under extreme conditions is the rigorous definition of what constitutes an ``extreme event'' in wind power forecasting \citep{sideratos2012extreme, liu2024extreme}. In this study, extreme events do not denote a single named meteorological subtype, such as typhoon, icing, or a specific ramping pattern. Instead, they refer to a unified target domain composed of rare, high-risk, high-volatility, and out-of-distribution operating states induced by extreme meteorological deviations and their associated turbine responses relative to the normal-operating domain, consistent with transfer-learning settings in which the source and target domains differ through their marginal distributions and operational regimes \citep{pan2010survey, bendavid2010theory}. To construct this target domain, a physics-statistics hybrid screening strategy is adopted: physical thresholding captures deterministic high-wind shutdown risk, whereas percentile-based rules identify statistically rare meteorological deviations at each wind farm, following the broader logic of mixed rule-and-statistics criteria used in recent extreme-event energy data studies \citep{liu2023eweld}. A sample is classified as belonging to the target domain if it satisfies any of the following criteria:
\end{quote}

The target domain is the union of these subsets, and the remaining eligible observations form the source domain. % BEGIN VERIFIED CHANGE event_subgroups
\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Meteorological-Extreme Domain Definition'', near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
No further subdivision of extreme-event samples into multiple subclasses is attempted. This choice is deliberate because extreme events are inherently scarce in realistic forecasting settings; splitting them into fine-grained categories would substantially weaken the statistical support available for transfer learning and would turn a small-sample problem into a near-few-shot problem, a difficulty also reported in recent extreme-condition wind power studies \citep{liang2025coldwave}. From the perspective of domain adaptation, these heterogeneous extreme states share the same modeling characteristic: they are all out-of-distribution samples exhibiting elevated volatility, non-stationarity, and clear deviation from normal operating patterns \citep{pan2010survey, bendavid2010theory}. The objective of TL-QLDMR is therefore to learn a unified disturbance-robust adaptation mechanism rather than a separate submodel for each rare event type. The union of the above three rules thus forms a single target domain that is physically interpretable, statistically sufficient for model training, and consistent with the data-scarce nature of extreme-event forecasting. All remaining samples constitute the normal-operating source domain.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The target-domain fitting and evaluation rows are defined by the union of these subsets; source-inclusive methods additionally use the stated normal-domain source rows. Evaluation also separates high-wind, low-temperature, and high-temperature observations, allowing overlap and reporting the corresponding counts. Membership is determined retrospectively from weather at the forecast target time, whereas predictors use only earlier measurements. The task is therefore next-step power prediction conditional on meteorological-tail membership, rather than prediction of a named-event or tail-state onset.}
\end{quote}

% BEGIN VERIFIED CHANGE chronological_protocol
\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Chronological protocol'', the opening paragraphs:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
No corresponding passage appears in the original manuscript. The following text is added in the chronological evaluation subsection of the revised manuscript.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The experiments use the supplied original workbooks with chronological separation of fitting, validation, calibration, and testing. Model fitting uses 1 January--31 December 2019. The first quarter of 2020 is the validation period: the independently tuned formal procedure comparison uses Q1 only for its frozen model-selection protocol, whereas the fixed-setting sensitivity analyses that follow do not use Q1 to select their common reference configuration. April--June 2020 (Q2) supplies interval-calibration labels for the procedure comparison, and July--December 2020 (Q3--Q4) supplies test labels. The procedure-comparison workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after its selection and analysis specifications are locked. The matched point analysis uses no Q2 label, and its configurations and analysis specification are locked before its Q3--Q4 evaluation. All boundaries are left-inclusive and right-exclusive at midnight. The forecast horizon is 15 minutes: each input contains the preceding 24 observations, with consecutive input-to-input and last-input-to-target intervals of exactly 15 minutes. Adjacent windows on opposite sides of a period boundary may share already observed input rows, as in rolling forecasting, but every forecast target belongs to exactly one period. No Q1, Q2, or Q3--Q4 label enters the 2019 fit; no Q2 or Q3--Q4 label enters Q1 model selection; and no Q3--Q4 label enters fixed Q2 calibration. Past-only rolling calibration is evaluated separately: it can use Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed strictly before the current forecast and adds the current outcome only after issuing that forecast. Random sampling is confined to the 2019 fitting pool and to algorithmic landmark seeds; it does not create the calendar partitions.}

{\color{blue}The study uses two common meteorological input tracks across all six sites. The formal validation-selected comparison uses four wind speeds, temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sine/cosine encodings of four wind directions at each of the 24 strictly preceding observations, giving 15 variables per step and 360 flattened inputs. The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses retain the earlier track of four wind speeds, temperature, and the same eight directional encodings, giving 13 variables per step and 312 flattened inputs. Neither track uses past power or future meteorological values. Times written as 24:00 are normalized to the next day; all rows sharing an ambiguous duplicate timestamp are removed before chronological sorting. Missing codes ($-99$), nonfinite values, all-zero meteorological records, negative wind speeds, and directions outside $[0,360]$ are treated as missing covariates. Targets with missing power, hub wind, or temperature and windows with non-15-minute gaps are excluded by fixed rules. Other power values, including negative or above-capacity observations, are retained. Missing input values are replaced by lag-specific fitting means; an entirely missing coordinate uses zero. Feature standardization and capacity-normalized label standardization use only the observations actually fitted in that branch, excluding unused target labels in scarcity experiments. No future-value filling, clipping, or error-based exclusions are applied. The original files are preserved, although their upstream measurement and processing history is not fully documented.}

{\color{blue}Domain thresholds use valid meteorological observations from 2019 only. Farm~6 thresholds are 15.43\,m/s for wind and 10.24/31.36\,$^\circ$C for temperature; its training set contains 32,832 source and 2,076 target windows. Table~6 reports all six sites. Test membership is determined retrospectively from observed target-time weather; this protocol does not forecast event onset. The time split, missing-value rules, and common-setting comparison grids were specified before those fits. This is a temporal holdout within a previously studied public dataset.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE chronological_protocol

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Chronological protocol'', near the added passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
No corresponding passage appears in the original manuscript. The following text is added in the chronological evaluation subsection of the revised manuscript.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses use $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$, RBF bandwidth parameter $\gamma=0.003$, 256 requested landmarks, batch size 256, Adam learning rate 0.01, and 64 epochs, on an Intel Xeon Platinum 8452Y host with one computational thread (Python 3.10.9, NumPy 2.2.6, and scikit-learn 1.7.2). These values define a common reference configuration for probing model behavior; the formal comparison applies its separately frozen Q1 selection protocol. Unless varied explicitly, loss coefficients are $C_S=1000/(2n_S)$ and $C_T=1000/(2n_T)$, so both domains receive equal total coefficient mass and $n_SC_S+n_TC_T=1000$. Target-only fitting uses $C_T=1000/n_T$, centered target residual variance, no projected discrepancy, and its own fitting statistics and landmarks. Its epochs are raised to the smallest integer giving at least as many Adam updates as the paired full model; equal update opportunities do not certify equal optimization accuracy. The full, no-variance, no-discrepancy, and target-only variants use seeds 0, 1, and 2. These are algorithmic repeats on a shared test period, not independent datasets or confidence intervals.}

{\color{blue}Point prediction uses $\tau=0.5$. Interval fits use $\tau_L=0.025$ and $\tau_U=0.975$. Define ordered endpoints $\ell(x)=\min\{f_{\tau_L}(x),f_{\tau_U}(x)\}$ and $u(x)=\max\{f_{\tau_L}(x),f_{\tau_U}(x)\}$. Calibration scores are $s_i=\max\{\ell(x_i)-y_i,y_i-u(x_i),0\}$. With $\alpha=0.05$, set $k=\lceil(n_{\rm cal}+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$, $q=s_{(k)}$, and report $[\ell(x)-q,u(x)+q]$. A finite interval requires $k\le n_{\rm cal}$. On Farm~6, $n_{\rm cal}=225$ and $k=215$. This formula defines the fixed Q2 expansion, to which no Q3--Q4 label contributes. The separately reported past-only rolling expansion may use only Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed before each forecast; it never uses the current or a future outcome. These are empirical temporal evaluations without an exchangeability or conditional-coverage guarantee \citep{romano2019cqr}.}

{\color{blue}Each branch saves source/target fitting identifiers, preprocessing statistics, landmarks, model coefficients, calibration scores, and individual test predictions. Code and workbook hashes accompany the fixed protocol. Reported fitting time includes landmark selection, feature construction, regularizer construction, and Adam, but excludes workbook loading, preprocessing, prediction, and post-fit objective diagnostics. Timings are wall-clock measurements from a shared compute host. Seed ranges throughout these analyses describe algorithmic variation rather than confidence intervals; fitting times do not represent inference or deployment latency.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE chronological_settings

\par\noindent\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Fixed-setting cross-farm sensitivity}}\par
{\color{blue}Each site is evaluated as the target in turn. Sources are 2019 normal-domain observations from the other five sites, capped at 6,000 per source site by deterministic time-even subsampling (30,000 in total). A seed-0 subset of 128 target-site training-period meteorological-tail labels supports supervised adaptation. Power is normalized by the corresponding site's capacity before common fitting-only standardization, and predictions are converted back to the target site's MW scale. The paired target-only fit uses exactly the same target fitting labels, its own preprocessing and landmarks, and at least the full model's number of Adam updates. The effective feature dimensions are 256 for the full model and 128 for target-only fitting, which has only 128 fitting inputs. Both receive 7,552 Adam updates. These compare complete fitting procedures, including different preprocessing, feature maps, and residual-variance domains; they do not isolate a causal effect of adding source labels. All target calibration labels are additional to the 128 fitting labels and are counted in the interval table. This is supervised cross-farm adaptation, not transfer to a site with no labeled target data. Full/target-only RMSE pairs for sites 1--6 are 19.880752/23.218175, 27.819462/24.956039, 11.485825/14.297631, 5.302804/6.559925, 10.702967/17.443978, and 13.775753/13.097317 MW. The source-inclusive Full procedure has lower test RMSE on four sites and higher test RMSE on sites 2 and 6 at this fixed setting. Full-model interval coverage ranges from 0.563889 on site 5 to 1.000000 on site 4, despite the nominal calibration target of 0.95. The gains and losses demonstrate heterogeneous transfer behavior, while the coverage variation reveals substantial temporal calibration error on some sites.}

% -------------Reviewer 1, Concern 11--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 1, Concern 11}}}
\emph{The literature review section should be significantly expanded and structured more critically, using these papers for example ``Multiscale Wind Forecasting Using Explainable-Adaptive Hybrid Deep Learning'', ``Prediction of uncertainty ramping demand in new power systems based on a CNN-LSTM hybrid neural network'', ``Wind power forecasting enhancement utilizing adaptive quantile function and CNN-LSTM: A probabilistic approach'', ``A multi-level model for hybrid short term wind forecasting based on SVM, wavelet transform and feature selection''.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We expanded the Introduction and Related Work into a critical comparison rather than a list of citations. The revision discusses all four suggested studies: the wavelet--SVM model as a multiscale point predictor; the adaptive-quantile CNN--LSTM as probabilistic wind-power forecasting; the explainable multiscale CNN--BiLSTM as regional wind-speed forecasting; and the CNN--LSTM uncertainty model as net-load ramping-demand prediction. The last two address related but different targets from scarce-label, cross-domain meteorological-extreme wind-power prediction. We compare representation capacity and data, optimization, and tuning demands with the auditable convex fixed-feature objective and its kernel/rank dependence. The manuscript also states that convexity and fixed features do not establish interpretability because no feature-attribution, sensitivity, physical-consistency, or operational explanation study is provided. This positioning motivates the formulation without claiming general superiority or empirical interpretability.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised the Introduction roadmap and opening of Related Work, added a dedicated critical-comparison subsection, and removed the unsupported implication that a fixed kernel model is empirically interpretable.

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Related Work'', subsection ``Wind forecasting under variability and uncertainty'':}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
The original Related Work section had no dedicated critical review of recent wind forecasting under variability and uncertainty. The following subsection has been added.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\textbf{Wind forecasting under variability and uncertainty}
{\color{blue}Hybrid signal-processing models explicitly separate temporal scales before prediction. For example, \citet{abedinia2022multilevel} combine wavelet decomposition, entropy-based feature selection, and SVM for short-term wind forecasting. This construction can improve a point predictor by filtering and selecting multiscale components, but it neither estimates a predictive distribution nor studies supervised transfer from normal to rare operating conditions. Deep architectures instead learn temporal representations: recent spatio-temporal and diffusion models increase expressive capacity for wind-power forecasting \citep{liu2025diffusion,zhang2026gwsstnet}, while transfer networks reuse representations across wind-power domains \citep{yin2021serioparallel,dong2023mdan}. Their flexibility is useful for complex temporal structure, but model capacity, training data, optimization, and tuning protocol remain part of the empirical comparison rather than an automatic advantage.}

{\color{blue}Probabilistic work has moved beyond a single fixed interval. \citet{abedinia2024quantile} estimate a wind-power quantile function with a CNN--LSTM and optimize a CRPS-based criterion. \citet{serttas2026multiscale} combine adaptive variational mode decomposition, a dual-stream CNN--BiLSTM, quantile outputs, and SHAP explanations for regional wind-speed forecasting. \citet{yu2025ramping} use CNN--LSTM quantile prediction for uncertain net-load ramping demand. The latter two tasks concern wind speed and system ramping demand, respectively, rather than cross-domain extreme-condition wind-power output. Conformalized regression forests and related methods add marginal coverage control to regional wind-power intervals \citep{jonkers2024regional,romano2019cqr}, although temporal dependence and distribution shift require assumptions beyond the nominal calibration formula.}

{\color{blue}These strands motivate a narrower role for the present kernel formulation. Fixed kernel or Nystr\"{o}m features permit a convex quantile objective and numerical primal--dual checks, which is useful when target labels are scarce. They do not learn multiscale or spatial representations automatically, and their performance depends on the kernel, rank, regularization, and source--target relation. We therefore compare against both kernel and tree alternatives and treat deep representation learning as a complementary approach rather than claim general superiority for kernel regression. Convexity and a fixed feature map make the optimization objective auditable, but do not by themselves make input effects interpretable. We do not present feature attributions, input-sensitivity maps, physical-consistency constraints, or operational explanation examples, and therefore make no empirical interpretability claim.}
\end{quote}

\phantomsection\section*{\textbf{REVIEWER 2}}\ResponseNativeLabel{rev2}}

{\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\underline{General Comments}}
\emph{The manuscript proposes Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR) for wind power forecasting under extreme operating conditions. The topic is timely and relevant to Energy. Forecasting under rare, high-risk wind-power regimes is important for renewable-energy integration and grid operation, and the attempt to combine transfer learning, quantile regression, large-margin distribution learning, and a scalable Nystrom-SGD solver is technically interesting. Several points need clarification and additional evidence before the main claims can be fully assessed, especially the experimental scope, data-splitting protocol, baseline reproducibility, and the strength of the theoretical and deployment-related claims.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
Thank you for identifying the central issues of experimental scope, chronology, baseline fairness, reproducibility, and claim strength. We rebuilt the main comparison as a frozen twelve-task, six-method study with 54 effective Q1 queries per method and task, complete task/seed reporting, locked Q3--Q4 evaluation, paired seven-day-block inference, and a matched component-removal analysis. In the primary within-site scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 3rd of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 5th of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. The Holm-significant scope-level TL-QLDMR relations were: In the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 4.178 percentage points higher than HistGBR; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$). In the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 0.511 percentage points higher than No variance; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). These tests concern the prespecified macro endpoint; empirical ordering by itself is not a significance claim. The Holm-significant TL-QLDMR comparisons were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.539, -0.139]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $204.912$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[71.894, 425.012]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.012$). Farm~3 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $71.623$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[35.870, 114.080]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.011$). Farm~1 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $214.556$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[91.628, 413.791]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.001$). Farm~6 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $16.917$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[9.148, 27.398]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). All other predeclared TL-QLDMR comparisons were not significant after adjustment; this absence of rejection is not evidence of equal performance. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the within-site scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.870\% (mean rank 2.17); TL-QLDMR 18.090\% (mean rank 2.00); Weighted SVQR 19.813\% (mean rank 3.17); No discrepancy 19.963\% (mean rank 2.67). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the cross-site stress scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.671\% (mean rank 2.50); TL-QLDMR 17.694\% (mean rank 2.17); Weighted SVQR 17.702\% (mean rank 3.00); No discrepancy 17.715\% (mean rank 2.33). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. The Holm-significant conditional removal effects were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.524, -0.142]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.008$). Farm~6 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No discrepancy (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No discrepancy, $-4.432\times 10^{-5}$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-5.832\times 10^{-5}, -3.030\times 10^{-5}]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). The observed magnitude is practically negligible on the MW$^2$ scale. These contrasts hold the TL-QLDMR-selected configuration, fitting rows, preprocessing, landmarks, and feature map fixed; variants were not independently retuned, and a failure to reject does not establish equivalence. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. We report the six within-site tasks as the primary scope and the six leave-one-farm-out tasks as a secondary transfer-stress scope, and interpret first-tier membership as non-rejection rather than equivalence. We also corrected the mathematical description, added a certificate-based retry and ineligibility rule, withdrew real-time and universal-superiority claims, and prepared a verified reproducibility package with immutable locks and hashes. The separate Farm 6 probability study is clearly labeled exploratory reused-test evidence because its historical dependency freeze is incomplete.

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Abstract, near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
Accurate wind power forecasting under extreme events is critical for grid stability and renewable energy integration, yet remains a formidable challenge due to severe data scarcity and substantial distribution shifts between normal and extreme-event operating regimes. While kernel-based methods, particularly support vector regression and Large-margin Distribution Machine-based Regression (LDMR), have demonstrated strong performance in various regression tasks due to their theoretical guarantees and robustness on limited data, their application to extreme-event forecasting faces critical limitations: the i.i.d. assumption underlying standard kernel methods is fundamentally violated under cross-domain scenarios, and the symmetric variance minimization in LDMR implicitly encourages symmetric error distributions, which conflicts with the asymmetric nature of quantile-based interval prediction required for uncertainty quantification. To extend kernel-based regression to extreme-event forecasting, we propose Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR), which addresses these challenges through three synergistic innovations: (i) an asymmetric variance regularizer that preserves LDMR's distributional robustness while accommodating quantile-specific error asymmetry, (ii) a supervised transfer learning framework integrating maximum mean discrepancy for feature alignment and weighted pinball loss for label adaptation, enabling effective knowledge transfer from abundant normal-domain data to scarce extreme-event samples, and (iii) a scalable Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver reducing complexity from $O(N^3)$ to $O(T \cdot N \cdot m)$. Comprehensive experiments on six wind farms demonstrate that TL-QLDMR achieves competitive performance in both deterministic and probabilistic forecasting in the extreme-event domain, with superior reliability-sharpness trade-off and practical scalability, making it suitable for real-time applications where interpretability and theoretical guarantees are prioritized.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}Wind-power forecasting during meteorological extremes combines limited target labels with source--target distribution differences. We formulate the Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR) using symmetric centered source-residual variance, a projected predictive-mean discrepancy, and weighted pinball loss. A frozen chronological comparison uses 128 target fitting labels and separates six primary within-site tasks from six secondary leave-one-farm-out stress tasks. In the primary within-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 13.913\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 18.090\%, ranked 3rd of six, and was outside the conservative first tier. In the secondary cross-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 14.923\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 17.694\%, ranked 5th of six, and remained in the conservative first tier. First-tier membership is non-rejection of inferiority rather than equivalence or superiority. Of 60 Holm-adjusted task comparisons, 1 favored TL-QLDMR and 4 favored a comparator. With its settings held fixed, TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four in the primary matched scope and 2nd of four in the secondary matched scope; 2 Holm-adjusted removal effects favored TL-QLDMR and 0 favored a removal variant. TL-QLDMR had the lowest mean task rank in both matched scopes. The matched effects are conditional because the variants were not independently retuned. The public Q3--Q4 period had been examined previously, so these results are test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation and do not establish universal model superiority.}
\end{quote}

% -------------Reviewer 2, Major Comment 1--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 2, Major Comment 1}}}
\emph{The experimental scope is narrower than the claims. The manuscript uses six wind farms to define and rank domain shift, but the main deterministic prediction comparison, probabilistic interval evaluation, noise robustness test, ablation study, residual-density analysis, and scalability study are all reported on Farm 6. Since Farm 6 is selected as the farm with the largest composite shift, this is better described as a selected stress-test case, not as full six-farm validation. The authors should either report the main comparisons across all six farms, or at least representative high-, medium-, and low-shift farms, or clearly narrow the claims to a Farm 6 evaluation after six-farm screening.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We no longer present Farm 6 screening as full six-farm validation. The principal point comparison now has two explicitly separated scopes. The primary scope consists of six within-site normal-to-extreme tasks, one per farm. The secondary scope consists of six leave-one-farm-out transfer-stress tasks. Each task uses 128 stratified target fitting labels, all six methods, and every prescribed evaluation seed. Results are reported for every site and summarized within each scope by site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE and average task rank. In the primary within-site scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 3rd of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 5th of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. The first-tier set is a conservative non-rejection summary and does not establish statistical equivalence.

The detailed fixed-setting Farm 6 component, weighting, scarcity, tail-definition, probability, and scalability experiments remain useful sensitivity analyses, but they are labeled separately and do not determine the formal scope-level conclusion. The new twelve-task comparison uses a public-data Q3--Q4 period that had been examined earlier, so it is leakage-controlled reused-test evidence rather than external confirmation. The resulting claims are limited to supervised adaptation with the stated target-label budget, farms, periods, and shift definitions.
