% -------------Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 4--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 4}}}
\emph{Some baseline choices need justification. For example, ARA-SVR appears to come from traffic-flow forecasting rather than wind-power forecasting.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We agree that ARA-SVR originated outside wind-power forecasting and that the historical comparison did not document an auditable equal-tuning protocol. We removed ARA-SVR together with the unauditable many-baseline result table and its superiority claim. The replacement comparison uses TL-QLDMR, its no-variance and no-discrepancy procedures, pooled weighted SVQR, target-only SVQR, and HistGBR. These choices directly distinguish the complete objective, its two regularizers, pooled kernel quantile regression, target-only training, and a strong non-kernel tree comparator.

For each task--method pair, the common frozen rule issues 54 effective Q1 configuration queries in three sequential stages; all data access, candidate generation, validation criteria, ranks, selected settings, seeds, and software implementations are documented. Kernel candidates are selected by three-seed mean Q1 RMSE of the $\tau=0.5$ fit and must satisfy the stated certificate rule; HistGBR is deterministic. In the primary within-site scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 3rd of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 5th of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. The Holm-significant scope-level TL-QLDMR relations were: In the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 4.178 percentage points higher than HistGBR; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$). In the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 0.511 percentage points higher than No variance; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). These tests concern the prespecified macro endpoint; empirical ordering by itself is not a significance claim. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. The Holm-significant TL-QLDMR comparisons were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.539, -0.139]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $204.912$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[71.894, 425.012]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.012$). Farm~3 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $71.623$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[35.870, 114.080]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.011$). Farm~1 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $214.556$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[91.628, 413.791]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.001$). Farm~6 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $16.917$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[9.148, 27.398]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). All other predeclared TL-QLDMR comparisons were not significant after adjustment; this absence of rejection is not evidence of equal performance. Equal query counts provide a transparent common validation budget but do not imply equal capacity or computation.

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Validation-selected predictive comparison'', near the added passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
This validation-selected study and its corresponding protocol were not present in the original manuscript.

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\par\noindent\textbf{Validation-selected predictive comparison}\par
{\color{blue}We compare TL-QLDMR, its no-variance and no-discrepancy variants, pooled weighted support vector quantile regression (SVQR), target-only SVQR, and histogram gradient boosting with quantile loss (HistGBR). The six within-site normal-to-extreme tasks form the primary scope, and the six leave-one-farm-out tasks form a secondary transfer-stress scope. Every site and method is retained in its prespecified scope. Within each primary task, the source observations are normal-domain windows from the target farm; within each secondary task, normal-domain source observations come from the other five farms.}

{\color{blue}Each task uses exactly 128 extreme-domain target fitting labels selected deterministically from 2019. The cells are training month crossed with mutually exclusive cold, hot, and high-wind/cut-out categories, assigned in that priority order from target-time meteorological covariates within the fitting period only; power values are not used in acquisition. Each nonempty cell first receives one observation; the remaining labels are allocated by the largest-remainder rule in proportion to the cells' remaining capacities, and observations within a cell are chosen near equally spaced clock-time targets. A primary task uses at most 7,500 normal-domain source windows from the same farm, deterministically thinned in chronological order, whereas a secondary task uses at most 1,500 normal-domain source windows from each of the other five farms. The 128 labels are the model-fitting budget rather than the total target supervision. For Farms~1--6, the additional target-domain Q1 selection counts are 169, 617, 2,410, 212, 134, and 177, and the Q2 calibration counts are 305, 102, 862, 319, 362, and 225, respectively.}

{\color{blue}The formal-comparison input at each forecast contains four wind-speed measurements, sine and cosine encodings of four wind-direction measurements, temperature, atmospheric pressure, and relative humidity at each of the 24 strictly preceding 15-minute observations, giving 360 flattened meteorological inputs. Past power and future meteorological values are excluded. Power labels are divided by their farm-specific nominal capacity before fit-only label standardization and are mapped back to the target farm's MW scale for evaluation. Missing-value imputation and feature and label standardization are fitted only on the 2019 model-fitting rows. For pooled models, the source and target domains each contribute one half of the preprocessing weight; target-only preprocessing uses only its target fitting rows. Nystr\"om landmarks are constructed without labels from fitting inputs. A pooled landmark pool contains at most 2,000 source and 2,000 target rows and assigns total K-means weight one half to each domain; target-only construction uses only target fitting rows. K-means is used when the requested rank is smaller than the pool, while all pool rows are retained when the requested rank equals the pool size; any resulting effective-rank cap is recorded.}

{\color{blue}For each task--method pair, the frozen search rule issues 54 effective Q1 configuration queries through three predeclared sequential stages of 18 new queries: a base search, a middle active-regularizer search or method-equivalent refinement, and a local joint refinement. The middle stage either varies the active regularizer coefficients while retaining the base incumbent's other coordinates or applies a method-equivalent deterministic refinement around that incumbent; the joint stage is generated locally around the incumbent retained after the middle stage. Within a task--method pair, the 18 effective configurations in each stage are distinct from one another and from every earlier-stage query, giving 54 distinct effective queries across the three stages. Kernel candidates are scored by the mean target-Q1 RMSE of the $\tau=0.5$ fit across seeds 0, 1, and 2, whereas deterministic HistGBR is fitted once at seed 0 per query. The pooled kernel searches include requested Nystr\"om ranks 128, 256, and 512, and target-only SVQR uses ranks 32, 64, and 128. Inactive hyperparameter coordinates are ignored when effective-query uniqueness is checked. Equal query counts provide a common configuration-query budget; they do not imply equal model capacity, numbers of solver attempts, wall-clock cost, or exhaustive optimization.}

{\color{blue}Candidate generation, model fitting, preprocessing, landmark construction, and Q1 scoring are completed before the immutable selection lock is created, and the analysis specification is separately frozen before any formal-comparison Q3--Q4 output is read. Each locked configuration is refitted on the unchanged 2019 fitting rows; Q1 labels are not added to the fit. Q2 is reserved for interval calibration, and the formal workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after the selection and analysis locks and then evaluates it under the locked settings. Kernel settings use landmark seeds 0, 1, and 2, and deterministic HistGBR uses seed 0. No task, method, seed, or configuration is selected from Q2 or Q3--Q4 performance. Because the public-data test period had already been examined in earlier work, this design provides test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation.}

{\color{blue}Every kernel fit is first attempted for at most 3,000 ADMM iterations. The numerical certificate is checked every 25 iterations and requires $P-D\leq 10^{-7}+10^{-3}\max\{1,|P|,|D|\}$. If the first attempt misses this condition, a second attempt is warm-started from its returned best-primal $(\boldsymbol{w},b)$ incumbent, with freshly initialized split and dual states, and is allowed at most 12,000 additional ADMM iterations; the data, feature map, objective, and hyperparameters remain unchanged. The candidate remains in the audit record but is ineligible for selection if any required selection seed still misses the certificate. Under the original execution rule, a locked main-study or matched-ablation fit that still missed the certificate produced no retained result. This is a numerical primal--dual-gap certificate for the chosen fixed-feature objective, not an interval-arithmetic proof, a certificate of Nystr\"om approximation error, or a predictive-generalization guarantee.}

{\color{blue}One locked main-study fit exhausted these two attempts with a relative gap of 0.0010217, compared with the unchanged 0.001 tolerance. Before its Q3--Q4 predictive scores were inspected, we froze a performance-blind solver amendment that committed the hashes of all then-existing completion artifacts and the already frozen analysis specifications. For an otherwise exact locked main or matched fit with no completed result, the amendment permitted one further warm restart, from the same best-primal incumbent and fresh split and dual states, for at most 96,000 iterations under the same objective, data, feature map, hyperparameters, and certificate tolerance. No completed result could be replaced. The single triggering main-study fit then met the unchanged certificate; no matched-ablation fit required the amendment. Selection, calibration, prediction, and analysis rules were unchanged, and the original failed record, model, amendment lock, and completion sidecars are retained in the reproducibility package.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE selection_protocol

% -------------Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 5--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 5}}}
\emph{The input-window construction should be described more clearly, including lag variables, forecasting horizon, normalization, missing-value handling, and whether future meteorological variables are used.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
The revised manuscript now distinguishes the two documented meteorological input tracks. The frozen formal comparison uses 15 variables at each of the 24 strictly preceding 15-minute observations---four wind speeds, temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sine/cosine encodings of four wind directions---for 360 flattened inputs. The fixed-setting and legacy sensitivity analyses retain the earlier 13-variable track without pressure or humidity, for 312 flattened inputs. Neither track uses past power, future meteorological values, or future power values. Ambiguous duplicate timestamps and windows containing a non-15-minute gap are excluded by fixed rules. Invalid codes and nonfinite covariates are treated as missing, and the remaining missing inputs, feature scaling, and capacity-normalized label scaling are determined from the observations fitted in the corresponding branch only. Thus the one-step forecasting horizon, lag variables, normalization, missing-value handling, and information available at forecast time are explicit for both experimental tracks.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We expanded the data and chronological-protocol text to specify the horizon, lagged variables, direction encoding, missing-value handling, time-gap exclusions, and fitting-only normalization.

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Chronological protocol'', the opening paragraphs:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
No corresponding passage appears in the original manuscript. The following text is added in the chronological evaluation subsection of the revised manuscript.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The experiments use the supplied original workbooks with chronological separation of fitting, validation, calibration, and testing. Model fitting uses 1 January--31 December 2019. The first quarter of 2020 is the validation period: the independently tuned formal procedure comparison uses Q1 only for its frozen model-selection protocol, whereas the fixed-setting sensitivity analyses that follow do not use Q1 to select their common reference configuration. April--June 2020 (Q2) supplies interval-calibration labels for the procedure comparison, and July--December 2020 (Q3--Q4) supplies test labels. The procedure-comparison workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after its selection and analysis specifications are locked. The matched point analysis uses no Q2 label, and its configurations and analysis specification are locked before its Q3--Q4 evaluation. All boundaries are left-inclusive and right-exclusive at midnight. The forecast horizon is 15 minutes: each input contains the preceding 24 observations, with consecutive input-to-input and last-input-to-target intervals of exactly 15 minutes. Adjacent windows on opposite sides of a period boundary may share already observed input rows, as in rolling forecasting, but every forecast target belongs to exactly one period. No Q1, Q2, or Q3--Q4 label enters the 2019 fit; no Q2 or Q3--Q4 label enters Q1 model selection; and no Q3--Q4 label enters fixed Q2 calibration. Past-only rolling calibration is evaluated separately: it can use Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed strictly before the current forecast and adds the current outcome only after issuing that forecast. Random sampling is confined to the 2019 fitting pool and to algorithmic landmark seeds; it does not create the calendar partitions.}

{\color{blue}The study uses two common meteorological input tracks across all six sites. The formal validation-selected comparison uses four wind speeds, temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sine/cosine encodings of four wind directions at each of the 24 strictly preceding observations, giving 15 variables per step and 360 flattened inputs. The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses retain the earlier track of four wind speeds, temperature, and the same eight directional encodings, giving 13 variables per step and 312 flattened inputs. Neither track uses past power or future meteorological values. Times written as 24:00 are normalized to the next day; all rows sharing an ambiguous duplicate timestamp are removed before chronological sorting. Missing codes ($-99$), nonfinite values, all-zero meteorological records, negative wind speeds, and directions outside $[0,360]$ are treated as missing covariates. Targets with missing power, hub wind, or temperature and windows with non-15-minute gaps are excluded by fixed rules. Other power values, including negative or above-capacity observations, are retained. Missing input values are replaced by lag-specific fitting means; an entirely missing coordinate uses zero. Feature standardization and capacity-normalized label standardization use only the observations actually fitted in that branch, excluding unused target labels in scarcity experiments. No future-value filling, clipping, or error-based exclusions are applied. The original files are preserved, although their upstream measurement and processing history is not fully documented.}

{\color{blue}Domain thresholds use valid meteorological observations from 2019 only. Farm~6 thresholds are 15.43\,m/s for wind and 10.24/31.36\,$^\circ$C for temperature; its training set contains 32,832 source and 2,076 target windows. Table~6 reports all six sites. Test membership is determined retrospectively from observed target-time weather; this protocol does not forecast event onset. The time split, missing-value rules, and common-setting comparison grids were specified before those fits. This is a temporal holdout within a previously studied public dataset.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE chronological_protocol

At every site the fitted percentile wind threshold is below 25\,m/s, so the $>25$ rule is nested in W and adds no observation to the union. {\color{blue}For temporal description, an episode is a maximal sequence of union-member target timestamps exactly 15 minutes apart. Duration is the represented exposure, calculated as the number of retained 15-minute target slots times 0.25\,h; it therefore exceeds the difference between the last and first displayed timestamps by 0.25\,h. The P95 column uses the linearly interpolated empirical 95th percentile. Table~5 reports all such episodes and chooses the longest episode at each site as a reproducible representative; the earliest start breaks a duration tie, and prediction errors are never used. Seasonal entries are the percentages of that site's union windows in December--February, March--May, June--August, and September--November. At the detailed Farm~6 site, applying the same objective rule separately gives W: 2019-08-24 02:15--2019-08-24 17:30 (15.50\,h); C: 2019-02-16 18:30--2019-02-18 07:00 (36.75\,h); H: 2019-08-09 00:45--2019-08-09 19:00 (18.50\,h); no $>25$\,m/s episode occurs. These are descriptive sample episodes, not independently named storms. The domain definition does not include power-ramp events: ramp-risk forecasting would require a separately declared ramp magnitude, horizon, and onset target, and is outside the present next-step conditional power task.}

% -------------Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 7--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 7}}}
\emph{Figures 3--7 use selected temporal segments. The selection criterion should be stated to avoid the impression of cherry-picked examples.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We removed the old prediction plots whose displayed temporal segments lacked a defensible prespecified selection record. The main v2 figures are generated directly from the complete formal analysis and display all predefined farms and methods: one figure reports capacity-normalized RMSE across the six within-site tasks, and the companion figure reports the scope-level average ranks without filtering by test performance. The tables likewise retain every task, method, and prescribed seed, so the formal visual evidence cannot be chosen from favorable episodes. In the primary within-site scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 3rd of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 5th of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. The Holm-significant scope-level TL-QLDMR relations were: In the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 4.178 percentage points higher than HistGBR; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$). In the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 0.511 percentage points higher than No variance; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). These tests concern the prespecified macro endpoint; empirical ordering by itself is not a significance claim. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation.

Where a contiguous episode remains useful for describing meteorological event composition, the rule is objective and unrelated to model error: choose the longest qualifying episode at each site and use the earliest start as the tie-breaker. Its criterion and timestamps are stated explicitly. Such episode illustrations are descriptive sensitivity material and are not used to support the formal v2 ranking or inference.

\begin{quote}
\small
\par\noindent\textbf{Legacy exploratory multi-quantile analysis}\par
{\color{blue}The within-Farm~6 nine-quantile experiment is retained as a separate exploratory probability sensitivity analysis. It predates the frozen formal protocol and uses the earlier 13-variable, 24-lag input track, giving 312 meteorological inputs. In this track, pooled methods use 7,500 source fitting windows, and every method uses all 2,076 target fitting labels. The archived legacy artifacts label TL-QLDMR as ``Full''. The predefined quantile grid is}
\begin{equation*}
{\color{blue}\mathcal{T}=\{0.025,0.05,0.10,0.25,0.50,0.75,0.90,0.95,0.975\}.}
\end{equation*}

{\color{blue}Each kernel procedure receives one reference configuration $(\gamma,A,p,\lambda_1,\lambda_2)=(0.003,1000,0.5,1,1)$ and 15 fixed Latin-hypercube configurations. Their ranges are $\gamma\in[10^{-4},10^{-1}]$, total loss mass $A\in[10^2,10^5]$, target fraction $p\in[0.05,0.95]$, and active regularizer coefficients in $[10^{-2},10^3]$; all coordinates except $p$ use logarithmic scales. The Latin-hypercube design uses fixed seed 20261022, and every legacy kernel candidate uses 128 requested landmarks. Source and target loss coefficients are $C_S=A(1-p)/n_S$ and $C_T=Ap/n_T$, inactive regularizer coordinates are ignored, and target-only SVQR uses $p=1$ and $C_T=A/n_T$. With the same fixed seed, HistGBR receives 16 configurations sampled without replacement from the Cartesian grid formed by learning rates $\{0.03,0.1\}$, leaf limits $\{7,15,31\}$, minimum leaf counts $\{10,20,40\}$, $L_2$ weights $\{0,1,10\}$, iteration counts $\{100,200\}$, and target fractions $\{0.1,0.5,0.9\}$. This legacy track uses fitting-only equal-row preprocessing, so domain influence follows the available row counts, and ordinary unweighted K-means on the sampled landmark pool; it does not use the explicit one-half source/one-half target weights of the formal comparison.}

{\color{blue}Candidates are scored by unweighted mean Q1 pinball loss over all nine quantiles. Ties use the fixed candidate index, and the archived legacy rule does not filter candidates by convergence status. The 96 method--candidate records comprise 864 seed-0 quantile fits, and all six settings are locked before any Q2 calibration or Q3--Q4 prediction. The selected kernel settings are then evaluated at landmark seeds 0, 1, and 2, while deterministic HistGBR uses seed 0. Equal candidate counts specify this legacy probability-selection budget but do not imply equal model capacity or computational cost. The six selected settings are reported with the legacy audit material in Appendix Table~35.}

{\color{blue}Raw quantile forecasts are retained for quantile-specific pinball loss, empirical reliability, and crossing diagnostics. A fixed label-free monotone rearrangement sorts the nine forecasts within each row before nested intervals and the weighted interval score are calculated. Q2 scores provide a fixed split-conformal expansion separately for the 50\%, 80\%, 90\%, and 95\% central intervals. The past-only rolling rule starts from Q2, uses at most the 256 most recent scores available before each forecast, and appends the current Q3--Q4 score only after that forecast has been issued. No Q3--Q4 label selects a configuration or the monotone-rearrangement rule; the fixed expansion uses Q2 alone, whereas each rolling expansion may use outcomes revealed strictly before that forecast.}

{\color{blue}The archived selection lock records the six selected configurations, and the saved validation, calibration, and test artifacts are covered by a post-completion integrity inventory. The original run manifest did not freeze the temporal loader, the target-sampling helper, the source-workbook hashes, the chronological-reference manifest, or the complete software environment; it recorded only selected source hashes and the Python and NumPy versions. This legacy analysis also uses the previously examined Q3--Q4 period. We therefore classify it as legacy/post hoc exploratory evidence rather than part of the formal point comparison or matched component analysis; its pinball loss, WIS, reliability, crossing, coverage, width, and paired-WIS results do not provide independent confirmation.}

{\color{blue}Table~10 shows that HistGBR has the lowest raw nine-quantile mean pinball loss (1.767\,MW) and rearranged WIS (3.531\,MW), followed by target-only SVQR (1.995 and 3.971\,MW). TL-QLDMR (Full) gives 2.045 and 4.090\,MW. Its raw crossing rate is zero, as is that of the no-discrepancy variant, whereas the other four methods cross on 38.07\%--45.84\% of test rows. This ordering stability does not translate into the lowest proper score or calibration error: TL-QLDMR's rearranged reliability MACE is 8.66 percentage points, compared with 7.35 for the no-variance and weighted-SVQR fits. These results do not establish a general probabilistic advantage for the complete objective.}

{\color{blue}For TL-QLDMR (Full), fixed Q2 calibration gives PICP values 0.532, 0.894, 0.960, and 0.977 at nominal coverages 0.50, 0.80, 0.90, and 0.95, with widths 11.21, 30.86, 41.52, and 54.75\,MW (Table~11). Figure~4 reports all nine reliability points before and after rearrangement, while Fig.~5 shows the static coverage--width trade-off without selecting methods or levels by test performance. Past-only rolling results are retained in the table as a separate information setting.}

{\color{blue}Paired probability-score inference uses the same 25 seven-day calendar blocks. WIS is computed separately for every seed and forecast, then averaged across landmark seeds within that forecast before forming paired method differences. The WIS difference (TL-QLDMR minus comparator) is $-0.0009$\,MW against the no-discrepancy variant (95\% block-bootstrap interval $[-0.0014,-0.0004]$, Holm $p=0.0058$), a statistically detectable but practically negligible difference. Against HistGBR the difference is $0.5585$\,MW ($[0.3290,0.8272]$, Holm $p=0.0020$), favoring HistGBR. The other three adjusted comparisons are not significant. Table~12 retains all five effects and tests. The block bootstrap treats block effects as approximately independent and exchangeable; the sign-flip test additionally requires approximate sign symmetry under the null. The small number of blocks and reused test period therefore require conservative interpretation.}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par

\begin{quote}
\small
\textbf{Meteorological-tail domain composition}
{\color{blue}Table~4 describes all eligible 2019--2020 forecast targets before any model fitting. Here W denotes the site-specific upper-2\% wind rule, C and H the lower-2\% and upper-2\% temperature rules, and $>25$ the nominal 25\,m/s rule. The cold and hot rules are mutually exclusive, so the two displayed wind--temperature intersections report every possible overlap between the three base rules. At every site the fitted percentile wind threshold is below 25\,m/s, so the $>25$ rule is nested in W and adds no observation to the union. The union represents 3.79--9.87\% of eligible windows across sites; departures from 6\% reflect ties, cross-rule overlap, and temporal distribution shift relative to the 2019 threshold-fitting period.}

\begingroup
\centering
\par\noindent\textit{\textcolor{blue}{Composition of the sample-level meteorological target domain over all eligible 2019--2020 windows. Percentages in the last column use all eligible windows at that site as the denominator.}}

4 & 69,571 & 884 & 743 & 1,509 & 47 & 22 & 0 & 3,114 (4.48\%) \\

\endgroup

{\color{blue}For temporal description, an episode is a maximal sequence of union-member target timestamps exactly 15 minutes apart. Duration is the represented exposure, calculated as the number of retained 15-minute target slots times 0.25\,h; it therefore exceeds the difference between the last and first displayed timestamps by 0.25\,h. The P95 column uses the linearly interpolated empirical 95th percentile. Table~5 reports all such episodes and chooses the longest episode at each site as a reproducible representative; the earliest start breaks a duration tie, and prediction errors are never used. Seasonal entries are the percentages of that site's union windows in December--February, March--May, June--August, and September--November. At the detailed Farm~6 site, applying the same objective rule separately gives W: 2019-08-24 02:15--2019-08-24 17:30 (15.50\,h); C: 2019-02-16 18:30--2019-02-18 07:00 (36.75\,h); H: 2019-08-09 00:45--2019-08-09 19:00 (18.50\,h); no $>25$\,m/s episode occurs. These are descriptive sample episodes, not independently named storms. The domain definition does not include power-ramp events: ramp-risk forecasting would require a separately declared ramp magnitude, horizon, and onset target, and is outside the present next-step conditional power task.}

% -------------Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 8--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 8}}}
\emph{The residual-density comparison should include quantitative residual statistics, such as skewness, kurtosis, tail-error frequency, and calibration error.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We separate three kinds of evidence that the earlier presentation conflated. First, the formal v2 point comparison evaluates predictive error and paired temporal-block differences on all twelve tasks. Second, the frozen matched analysis estimates regularizer-removal effects while holding the Full-selected configuration, rows, preprocessing, landmarks, feature map, and non-regularizer hyperparameters fixed. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the within-site scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.870\% (mean rank 2.17); TL-QLDMR 18.090\% (mean rank 2.00); Weighted SVQR 19.813\% (mean rank 3.17); No discrepancy 19.963\% (mean rank 2.67). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the cross-site stress scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.671\% (mean rank 2.50); TL-QLDMR 17.694\% (mean rank 2.17); Weighted SVQR 17.702\% (mean rank 3.00); No discrepancy 17.715\% (mean rank 2.33). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. The Holm-significant conditional removal effects were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.524, -0.142]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.008$). Farm~6 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No discrepancy (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No discrepancy, $-4.432\times 10^{-5}$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-5.832\times 10^{-5}, -3.030\times 10^{-5}]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). The observed magnitude is practically negligible on the MW$^2$ scale. These contrasts hold the TL-QLDMR-selected configuration, fitting rows, preprocessing, landmarks, and feature map fixed; variants were not independently retuned, and a failure to reject does not establish equivalence. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. Third, any retained residual table reports numerical mean, spread, skewness, excess kurtosis, tail-error frequency, and absolute-error quantiles only as a legacy reused-test diagnostic.

The residual statistics are not used for model selection, formal component attribution, or a claim that a visually concentrated density causes better forecasting. In the retained Farm 6 diagnostic, for example, the full model has skewness $-2.908$, excess kurtosis 16.459, and a 6.34\% frequency of $|e|>19.2$ MW, whereas HistGBR has a 5.73\% tail-error frequency. Calibration error belongs to the separate nine-quantile probability analysis, which reports reliability, crossing, pinball loss, and WIS but has an incomplete historical dependency freeze. This organization supplies the requested quantitative diagnostics while preventing them from being used as evidence for a different objective or for formal v2 superiority.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We added and removed the relevant text in Section ``Experiments''. The exact original wording and revised text are reproduced below at each approximate location.

\begin{quote}
\small
\subsection{Experiment 4: Ablation Study}\label{sec:exp4}

To validate the contribution of the three core components (transfer learning, LDMR variance regularization, and MMD feature alignment), this ablation experiment evaluates structurally reduced variants on both point and interval tasks. Additionally, to verify the necessity of asymmetric variance regularization for quantile regression, we include LDMR-Quantile (SymVar), which replaces the asymmetric variance term with standard symmetric variance minimization while retaining the transfer learning framework.

The full TL-QLDMR framework is compared against four architectural reductions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{LDMR-Quantile (SymVar)}: Replaces asymmetric variance regularization with symmetric variance minimization, testing whether the asymmetry is necessary for quantile-specific calibration.
    \item \textbf{w/o Transfer (Target-only quantile LDMR, QLDMR)}: Trained exclusively on extreme-event target samples without source-domain integration or MMD alignment.
    \item \textbf{w/o LDMR (Variance Penalty)}: The asymmetric variance regularizer is removed, deteriorating the framework into a generalized Transfer SVR/SVQR variant that lacks distributional robustness.
    \item \textbf{w/o MMD (Feature Alignment)}: The algorithm employs cross-domain training data but disables MMD alignment, relying purely on weighted objective loss.
\end{enumerate}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation_results} reports the ablation results on Farm~6. The full TL-QLDMR consistently attains the best deterministic and probabilistic performance, indicating that all three components contribute non-trivially to final accuracy and calibration quality.

w/o Transfer            & 7.930 & 0.9497 & 0.952 & 26.891 & 0.2797 & 0.2797 \\

w/o MMD                 & 7.745 & 0.9520 & 0.947 & 26.049 & 0.2710 & 0.3528 \\
\textbf{TL-QLDMR (Full)} & \textbf{7.476} & \textbf{0.9557} & \textbf{0.959} & \textbf{25.791} & \textbf{0.2683} & \textbf{0.2683} \\

\begin{center}
\captionsetup{type=figure,hypcap=false}
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth]{experiment4/plots/residual_distribution.png}
\captionof{figure}{Residual density comparison between TL-QLDMR and ablated variants on the Farm~6 test set.}
\label{fig:ablation_residual}
\end{center}

The ablation outcomes confirm that each component contributes materially to robustness. Removing transfer learning reduces both point accuracy ($R^2$: 0.9557 $\rightarrow$ 0.9497) and interval quality (CWC: 0.2683 $\rightarrow$ 0.2797), indicating that target-only training is insufficient under strong domain shift. Removing LDMR regularization or MMD alignment causes clear interval-quality degradation (CWC rises to 0.3507 and 0.3528), even when point-metric changes are smaller, showing that residual-shape control and feature alignment are central to reliable uncertainty estimation.

Critically, the LDMR-Quantile (SymVar) variant, which replaces asymmetric variance with symmetric variance minimization, exhibits degraded performance on both point prediction (RMSE: 7.868 vs. 7.476) and interval prediction (CWC: 0.3029 vs. 0.2683, PINAW: 0.3029 vs. 0.2683). This degradation empirically validates our theoretical analysis in Section~\ref{novel}: symmetric variance minimization, while effective for mean regression, conflicts with the asymmetric residual distribution required for accurate quantile estimation. The symmetric regularizer forces errors toward a centered, Gaussian-like distribution, thereby degrading interval calibration at non-median quantiles.

The residual-density comparison in Fig.~\ref{fig:ablation_residual} supports this conclusion by showing tighter central concentration and weaker heavy tails for the full TL-QLDMR model; some ablated variants exhibit sharper central peaks but noticeably thicker tails, which corresponds to a higher probability of large-error events.

% BEGIN VERIFIED CHANGE metric_definitions
\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Evaluation measures'':}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
RMSE and MAE quantify the magnitude of prediction errors, while $R^2$ measures the proportion of variance explained by the model.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}Point prediction is evaluated by root mean squared error (RMSE), mean absolute error (MAE), and $R^2=1-\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2/\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$. Test $R^2$ can be negative when prediction error exceeds that of the test-mean reference. For a quantile forecast $q_\tau$ and residual $r=y-q_\tau$, the pinball loss is $\rho_\tau(r)=r\{\tau-\mathbf{1}(r<0)\}$. We report its mean at each of nine quantiles and their unweighted average. This aggregate remains defined when independently fitted quantiles cross. Reliability at level $\tau$ is summarized by the empirical cumulative probability $\widehat p_\tau=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{y_i\le q_\tau(x_i)\}$ and the mean absolute calibration error $J^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^J|\widehat p_{\tau_j}-\tau_j|$. The quantile-crossing rate is the fraction of rows having any adjacent decrease.}

{\color{blue}For a central interval $[\ell,u]$ with miscoverage $\alpha$, the interval score is}
\begin{equation}
{\color{blue}
\operatorname{IS}_{\alpha}(y,\ell,u)=(u-\ell)+\frac{2}{\alpha}(\ell-y)\mathbf{1}\{y<\ell\}+\frac{2}{\alpha}(y-u)\mathbf{1}\{y>u\}.}
\end{equation}
{\color{blue}Its sample mean is the Winkler score. Prediction interval coverage probability (PICP) is the covered fraction and mean prediction interval width (MPIW) is $n^{-1}\sum_i(u_i-\ell_i)$. For $K=4$ central intervals with $\alpha_k\in\{0.50,0.20,0.10,0.05\}$ and median $m$, the weighted interval score is}
\begin{equation}
{\color{blue}
\operatorname{WIS}=\frac{0.5|y-m|+\sum_{k=1}^{K}(\alpha_k/2)\operatorname{IS}_{\alpha_k}}{K+0.5}.}
\end{equation}
{\color{blue}Nine independently fitted quantiles are retained for the raw pinball and crossing diagnostics, then sorted within each forecast row by a fixed label-free monotone rearrangement \citep{chernozhukov2010rearrangement} before direct-quantile WIS and nested-interval evaluation. Raw and rearranged reliability curves are both reported; the score table retains raw mean pinball loss and crossing together with rearranged WIS and calibration error. The Q2-expanded intervals are evaluated separately through PICP, MPIW, and Winkler score and are not used to compute WIS. Width, interval score, and WIS are expressed in MW; lower values are preferable when interpreted together with reliability. The primary evaluation does not use the coverage--width criterion (CWC), whose thresholded penalty and normalization depend on user-selected constants; it instead gives PICP and MPIW separately and uses the proper interval and weighted interval scores. Where reported for historical comparisons, PINAW divides mean width by the observed test-label range rather than farm capacity.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE metric_definitions

\emph{The term ``extreme events'' should be used consistently. The current definition is sample-level out-of-distribution operating states, not necessarily named or tracked meteorological events.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We revised the title, keywords, domain-definition subsection, notation note, and Conclusion to distinguish the constructed task from named meteorological events. The preferred term is now ``meteorological extremes'' or ``meteorological-extreme conditions.'' Where ``extreme-event sample'' remains as shorthand, the manuscript defines it strictly as a forecast target satisfying a sample-level wind or temperature tail rule. It explicitly states that no independently identified storm, heat wave, cold wave, turbine shutdown event, or ramp event is inferred. The new composition analysis consequently calls contiguous runs ``sample episodes'' and does not treat them as independent storms.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised and added the relevant text in Manuscript title, Keywords, Section ``Proposed Method'', Section ``Experiments'', and the related passages listed below. The exact original wording and revised text are reproduced below at each approximate location.

A critical prerequisite for evaluating transfer learning under extreme conditions is the rigorous definition of what constitutes an ``extreme event'' in wind power forecasting \citep{sideratos2012extreme, liu2024extreme}. Instead, they refer to a unified target domain composed of rare, high-risk, high-volatility, and out-of-distribution operating states induced by extreme meteorological deviations and their associated turbine responses relative to the normal-operating domain, consistent with transfer-learning settings in which the source and target domains differ through their marginal distributions and operational regimes \citep{pan2010survey, bendavid2010theory}. A sample is classified as belonging to the target domain if it satisfies any of the following criteria:
\end{quote}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Meteorological-Extreme Domain Definition'', near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
No further subdivision of extreme-event samples into multiple subclasses is attempted. This choice is deliberate because extreme events are inherently scarce in realistic forecasting settings; splitting them into fine-grained categories would substantially weaken the statistical support available for transfer learning and would turn a small-sample problem into a near-few-shot problem, a difficulty also reported in recent extreme-condition wind power studies \citep{liang2025coldwave}. From the perspective of domain adaptation, these heterogeneous extreme states share the same modeling characteristic: they are all out-of-distribution samples exhibiting elevated volatility, non-stationarity, and clear deviation from normal operating patterns \citep{pan2010survey, bendavid2010theory}. The objective of TL-QLDMR is therefore to learn a unified disturbance-robust adaptation mechanism rather than a separate submodel for each rare event type. The union of the above three rules thus forms a single target domain that is physically interpretable, statistically sufficient for model training, and consistent with the data-scarce nature of extreme-event forecasting. All remaining samples constitute the normal-operating source domain.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The target-domain fitting and evaluation rows are defined by the union of these subsets; source-inclusive methods additionally use the stated normal-domain source rows. Evaluation also separates high-wind, low-temperature, and high-temperature observations, allowing overlap and reporting the corresponding counts. Membership is determined retrospectively from weather at the forecast target time, whereas predictors use only earlier measurements. The task is therefore next-step power prediction conditional on meteorological-tail membership, rather than prediction of a named-event or tail-state onset.}
\end{quote}

This paper presents TL-QLDMR for wind power forecasting under extreme events, where target-domain samples are limited and distribution shift is pronounced. {\color{blue}This paper presents TL-QLDMR for wind power forecasting when labeled target-domain samples are limited and the source and target samples are defined by different meteorological selection rules. The formulation combines normalized source-residual variance, a projected inter-domain mean-discrepancy penalty, and weighted pinball loss. The variance is symmetric; quantile dependence comes from the loss. Exact-kernel and fixed Nystr\"{o}m objectives are convex under the stated kernel and parameter conditions, without a claim of joint strong convexity or a convergence rate for Adam.}
\end{quote}

% -------------Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 12--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 2, Minor Comment 12}}}
\emph{The conclusion should include limitations, including the single-farm main evaluation, sample-level extreme-event definition, need for chronological validation, and lack of deployment-latency evidence.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
The revised evidence presentation now follows the formal hierarchy rather than a single-farm narrative. The Conclusion summarizes the scope-level macro results, task-comparison counts, matched aggregate results, and limitations; the Experiments section reports the individual favorable and adverse comparisons. Specifically, the revised manuscript reports the following results. In the primary within-site scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 3rd of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 5th of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the within-site scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.870\% (mean rank 2.17); TL-QLDMR 18.090\% (mean rank 2.00); Weighted SVQR 19.813\% (mean rank 3.17); No discrepancy 19.963\% (mean rank 2.67). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the cross-site stress scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.671\% (mean rank 2.50); TL-QLDMR 17.694\% (mean rank 2.17); Weighted SVQR 17.702\% (mean rank 3.00); No discrepancy 17.715\% (mean rank 2.33). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. The Holm-significant conditional removal effects were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.524, -0.142]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.008$). Farm~6 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No discrepancy (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No discrepancy, $-4.432\times 10^{-5}$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-5.832\times 10^{-5}, -3.030\times 10^{-5}]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). The observed magnitude is practically negligible on the MW$^2$ scale. These contrasts hold the TL-QLDMR-selected configuration, fitting rows, preprocessing, landmarks, and feature map fixed; variants were not independently retuned, and a failure to reject does not establish equivalence. The Holm-significant scope-level TL-QLDMR relations were: In the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 4.178 percentage points higher than HistGBR; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$). In the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 0.511 percentage points higher than No variance; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). These tests concern the prespecified macro endpoint; empirical ordering by itself is not a significance claim. The Holm-significant TL-QLDMR comparisons were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.539, -0.139]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $204.912$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[71.894, 425.012]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.012$). Farm~3 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $71.623$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[35.870, 114.080]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.011$). Farm~1 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $214.556$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[91.628, 413.791]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.001$). Farm~6 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $16.917$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[9.148, 27.398]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). All other predeclared TL-QLDMR comparisons were not significant after adjustment; this absence of rejection is not evidence of equal performance. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. The Experiments section states every Holm-adjusted favorable and unfavorable TL-QLDMR comparison supported by the analysis. First-tier membership is described as non-rejection of inferiority and not as equivalence. The earlier Farm 6 component, scarcity, weighting, tail-definition, probability, and scalability findings are grouped separately as sensitivity evidence.

The Limitations paragraph states that the study uses supervised target labels and extra Q1/Q2 labels; reuses a public-data test period without an external confirmation dataset; assigns meteorological-tail membership retrospectively; contains serial dependence; uses finite equal-query searches with unequal model capacity and computation; treats seeds as algorithmic repeats; certifies only the chosen fixed-feature objective; does not bound Nystr\"om approximation error; and does not validate deployment latency. It also states that matched effects are conditional, non-rejection is not equivalence, and the legacy probability dependency freeze is incomplete.

\color{black}

We revised and added the relevant text in Sections ``Conclusion'' and ``Experiments''. The exact original wording and revised text are reproduced below at each approximate location.

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Conclusion'', near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
Experimental results show that TL-QLDMR delivers consistent gains in both deterministic and interval forecasting on the most challenging target farm. For point prediction, it achieves the best RMSE (7.478) and $R^2$ (0.9557). For 95\% interval prediction, it attains PICP $=0.959$ together with the best CWC (0.268), indicating a favorable reliability-sharpness trade-off. Under injected noise, TL-QLDMR remains the strongest model across reported point and interval metrics. In addition, the Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver provides practical scalability, completing the full uncapped training set ($N=69{,}737$) in 5.021 seconds, whereas CVXOPT, Torch-GD, and batch SGD do not remain computationally viable at the same scale.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The formal comparison uses a public six-farm dataset whose Q3--Q4 period had been examined before the frozen protocol was designed. Locking Q1 selection, the analysis specification, and the matched configurations before evaluation prevents further test-guided adaptation, but it does not turn the reused period into independent confirmation. The 128 target labels describe the fitting budget rather than total supervision because Q1 selection and Q2 calibration labels are additional; past-only rolling calibration further uses outcomes revealed before the current forecast. Equal configuration-query counts do not equalize model capacity, solver attempts, or wall-clock cost, algorithmic seed ranges are not confidence intervals, first-tier membership establishes non-rejection rather than equivalence, and matched removal effects are conditional on the TL-QLDMR-selected configuration. Chronological ordering does not remove serial dependence or establish conformal coverage guarantees. Meteorological-tail membership is defined retrospectively from target-time weather, with overlapping sample categories rather than independently tracked storms or ramp events. The numerical certificate applies only to each fixed-feature training objective, while Nystr\"{o}m approximation error, independent-farm generalization, longer forecast horizons, and deployment latency remain unestablished. The separate Farm~6 nine-quantile analysis is legacy exploratory evidence whose original archive did not freeze every current loader, sampler, or chronological-reference dependency.}
\end{quote}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Chronological protocol'', the opening paragraphs:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par

\small
No corresponding passage appears in the original manuscript. The following text is added in the chronological evaluation subsection of the revised manuscript.

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The experiments use the supplied original workbooks with chronological separation of fitting, validation, calibration, and testing. Model fitting uses 1 January--31 December 2019. The first quarter of 2020 is the validation period: the independently tuned formal procedure comparison uses Q1 only for its frozen model-selection protocol, whereas the fixed-setting sensitivity analyses that follow do not use Q1 to select their common reference configuration. April--June 2020 (Q2) supplies interval-calibration labels for the procedure comparison, and July--December 2020 (Q3--Q4) supplies test labels. The procedure-comparison workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after its selection and analysis specifications are locked. The matched point analysis uses no Q2 label, and its configurations and analysis specification are locked before its Q3--Q4 evaluation. All boundaries are left-inclusive and right-exclusive at midnight. The forecast horizon is 15 minutes: each input contains the preceding 24 observations, with consecutive input-to-input and last-input-to-target intervals of exactly 15 minutes. Adjacent windows on opposite sides of a period boundary may share already observed input rows, as in rolling forecasting, but every forecast target belongs to exactly one period. No Q1, Q2, or Q3--Q4 label enters the 2019 fit; no Q2 or Q3--Q4 label enters Q1 model selection; and no Q3--Q4 label enters fixed Q2 calibration. Past-only rolling calibration is evaluated separately: it can use Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed strictly before the current forecast and adds the current outcome only after issuing that forecast. Random sampling is confined to the 2019 fitting pool and to algorithmic landmark seeds; it does not create the calendar partitions.}

{\color{blue}The study uses two common meteorological input tracks across all six sites. The formal validation-selected comparison uses four wind speeds, temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sine/cosine encodings of four wind directions at each of the 24 strictly preceding observations, giving 15 variables per step and 360 flattened inputs. The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses retain the earlier track of four wind speeds, temperature, and the same eight directional encodings, giving 13 variables per step and 312 flattened inputs. Neither track uses past power or future meteorological values. Times written as 24:00 are normalized to the next day; all rows sharing an ambiguous duplicate timestamp are removed before chronological sorting. Missing codes ($-99$), nonfinite values, all-zero meteorological records, negative wind speeds, and directions outside $[0,360]$ are treated as missing covariates. Targets with missing power, hub wind, or temperature and windows with non-15-minute gaps are excluded by fixed rules. Other power values, including negative or above-capacity observations, are retained. Missing input values are replaced by lag-specific fitting means; an entirely missing coordinate uses zero. Feature standardization and capacity-normalized label standardization use only the observations actually fitted in that branch, excluding unused target labels in scarcity experiments. No future-value filling, clipping, or error-based exclusions are applied. The original files are preserved, although their upstream measurement and processing history is not fully documented.}

{\color{blue}Domain thresholds use valid meteorological observations from 2019 only. Farm~6 thresholds are 15.43\,m/s for wind and 10.24/31.36\,$^\circ$C for temperature; its training set contains 32,832 source and 2,076 target windows. Table~6 reports all six sites. Test membership is determined retrospectively from observed target-time weather; this protocol does not forecast event onset. The time split, missing-value rules, and common-setting comparison grids were specified before those fits. This is a temporal holdout within a previously studied public dataset.}
\end{quote}

{\color{black}
\phantomsection\section*{\textbf{REVIEWER 3}}\ResponseNativeLabel{rev3}}

{\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\underline{General Comments}}
\emph{This manuscript focuses on the challenges of limited samples, cross-domain distribution differences, and uncertainty quantification in wind power forecasting under extreme events. It proposes a TL-QLDMR framework integrating large-margin distribution learning, quantile regression, domain adaptation, and scalable optimization. The topic is practically relevant, the overall technical framework is reasonably complete, and the experiments cover point forecasting, interval forecasting, ablation studies, and computational efficiency.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
Thank you for recognizing the practical relevance and overall framework. We have clarified that the centered residual-variance term is symmetric, separated exact-kernel theory from the fixed-feature numerical implementation, and rebuilt the principal evidence as a frozen twelve-task comparison plus a matched component-removal analysis. In the primary within-site scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 13.913\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 18.090\%, an average task rank of 3.50, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 3rd of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the primary within-site scope contained HistGBR, No variance, and No discrepancy; TL-QLDMR was excluded ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was established for the macro RMSE endpoint. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. In the secondary cross-site stress scope, HistGBR was the empirical winner on the macro RMSE endpoint at 14.923\%. TL-QLDMR recorded a site-equal capacity-normalized RMSE of 17.694\%, an average task rank of 3.67, and 1 task win including ties, ranking 5th of six by the observed macro endpoint. The conservative first tier in the secondary cross-site stress scope contained HistGBR, No discrepancy, No variance, Weighted SVQR, and TL-QLDMR; TL-QLDMR was retained ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.336$), meaning that its inferiority to HistGBR was not established. Membership means that inferiority to the empirical winner was not established; it does not establish equivalence or equal performance. The Holm-significant scope-level TL-QLDMR relations were: In the primary within-site scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 4.178 percentage points higher than HistGBR; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.036$). In the secondary cross-site stress scope, TL-QLDMR's observed macro RMSE was 0.511 percentage points higher than No variance; the all-pairs difference was significant after Holm adjustment ($p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). These tests concern the prespecified macro endpoint; empirical ordering by itself is not a significance claim. The Holm-significant TL-QLDMR comparisons were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.539, -0.139]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.016$). Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $204.912$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[71.894, 425.012]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.012$). Farm~3 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $71.623$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[35.870, 114.080]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.011$). Farm~1 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than HistGBR (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus HistGBR, $214.556$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[91.628, 413.791]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.001$). Farm~6 (cross-site): TL-QLDMR had higher squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $16.917$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[9.148, 27.398]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). All other predeclared TL-QLDMR comparisons were not significant after adjustment; this absence of rejection is not evidence of equal performance. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the within-site scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.870\% (mean rank 2.17); TL-QLDMR 18.090\% (mean rank 2.00); Weighted SVQR 19.813\% (mean rank 3.17); No discrepancy 19.963\% (mean rank 2.67). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. Under the conditional matched-removal protocol in the cross-site stress scope, the four aggregate results were No variance 17.671\% (mean rank 2.50); TL-QLDMR 17.694\% (mean rank 2.17); Weighted SVQR 17.702\% (mean rank 3.00); No discrepancy 17.715\% (mean rank 2.33). TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four by observed macro RMSE. The Holm-significant conditional removal effects were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.524, -0.142]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.008$). Farm~6 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No discrepancy (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No discrepancy, $-4.432\times 10^{-5}$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-5.832\times 10^{-5}, -3.030\times 10^{-5}]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}<0.001$). The observed magnitude is practically negligible on the MW$^2$ scale. These contrasts hold the TL-QLDMR-selected configuration, fitting rows, preprocessing, landmarks, and feature map fixed; variants were not independently retuned, and a failure to reject does not establish equivalence. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. All predefined farms, methods, tasks, and seeds are retained; first-tier membership is reported only as non-rejection of inferiority. We also document coefficient mass rather than per-sample ratios alone, distinguish the older 312-input fixed-setting track from the 360-input v2 track, and provide auditable chronological splits and locks. The revised claims acknowledge reused-test status, conditional matched effects, the legacy probability provenance limit, lack of external confirmation, and unmeasured deployment latency.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised the Introduction, method, experiments, limitations, and Data and Code Availability statement; the exact changes relevant to each numbered concern are given below.

% -------------Reviewer 3, Concern 1--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 3, Concern 1}}}
\emph{The review of the existing literature on wind power forecasting under extreme events remains insufficient in the Introduction. After explaining the importance of extreme-event forecasting, the manuscript moves rather quickly to the general advantages of kernel methods and LDMR, without systematically discussing recent developments and limitations of deep learning, transfer learning, and probabilistic forecasting methods in extreme-event scenarios. Consequently, the motivation for adopting a kernel-based approach is not yet sufficiently clear. The authors are encouraged to expand the review of extreme-event wind power forecasting and explain the suitability, advantages, and potential trade-offs of kernel methods compared with neural networks or other learnable representation methods.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
The motivation now follows a structured comparison of recent wind forecasting under variability and uncertainty. We discuss multiscale signal decomposition, deep temporal and spatio-temporal representation learning, transfer networks, quantile-function forecasting, and conformalized wind-power intervals. We identify the requested wind-speed and net-load-ramping papers as related tasks rather than direct evidence on the present wind-power transfer problem. The kernel formulation is motivated by a convex fixed-feature quantile objective and numerical primal--dual checks when target labels are scarce. Its limits are stated alongside that motivation: it does not learn multiscale or spatial features automatically, and its behavior depends on kernel choice, Nystr\"{o}m rank, regularization, and the source--target relationship.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised the Introduction and added a critical Related Work subsection explaining recent extreme-condition and probabilistic forecasting developments and the advantages and trade-offs of fixed kernel features.

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\textbf{Wind forecasting under variability and uncertainty}
{\color{blue}Hybrid signal-processing models explicitly separate temporal scales before prediction. For example, \citet{abedinia2022multilevel} combine wavelet decomposition, entropy-based feature selection, and SVM for short-term wind forecasting. This construction can improve a point predictor by filtering and selecting multiscale components, but it neither estimates a predictive distribution nor studies supervised transfer from normal to rare operating conditions. Deep architectures instead learn temporal representations: recent spatio-temporal and diffusion models increase expressive capacity for wind-power forecasting \citep{liu2025diffusion,zhang2026gwsstnet}, while transfer networks reuse representations across wind-power domains \citep{yin2021serioparallel,dong2023mdan}. Their flexibility is useful for complex temporal structure, but model capacity, training data, optimization, and tuning protocol remain part of the empirical comparison rather than an automatic advantage.}

{\color{blue}Probabilistic work has moved beyond a single fixed interval. \citet{abedinia2024quantile} estimate a wind-power quantile function with a CNN--LSTM and optimize a CRPS-based criterion. \citet{serttas2026multiscale} combine adaptive variational mode decomposition, a dual-stream CNN--BiLSTM, quantile outputs, and SHAP explanations for regional wind-speed forecasting. \citet{yu2025ramping} use CNN--LSTM quantile prediction for uncertain net-load ramping demand. The latter two tasks concern wind speed and system ramping demand, respectively, rather than cross-domain extreme-condition wind-power output. Conformalized regression forests and related methods add marginal coverage control to regional wind-power intervals \citep{jonkers2024regional,romano2019cqr}, although temporal dependence and distribution shift require assumptions beyond the nominal calibration formula.}

{\color{blue}These strands motivate a narrower role for the present kernel formulation. Fixed kernel or Nystr\"{o}m features permit a convex quantile objective and numerical primal--dual checks, which is useful when target labels are scarce. They do not learn multiscale or spatial representations automatically, and their performance depends on the kernel, rank, regularization, and source--target relation. We therefore compare against both kernel and tree alternatives and treat deep representation learning as a complementary approach rather than claim general superiority for kernel regression. Convexity and a fixed feature map make the optimization objective auditable, but do not by themselves make input effects interpretable. We do not present feature attributions, input-sensitivity maps, physical-consistency constraints, or operational explanation examples, and therefore make no empirical interpretability claim.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE related_wind_forecasting

\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 3, Concern 2}}}
\emph{Please clarify how the source-domain mean residual in Eq.\ (4) is handled. According to its definition, this quantity is calculated from the model residuals and therefore appears to depend on the model parameters being optimized. However, the manuscript states that it is treated as a scalar constant during optimization. Meanwhile, the centered residual representation in Eq.\ (7) appears to imply that the mean residual is calculated from the current model. \subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
Your interpretation is correct: the source residual mean changes with $(w,b)$ and must not be held fixed. Substitution gives $H_S(y_S-\Phi_S^Tw-b\mathbf1)=H_S(y_S-\Phi_S^Tw)$ because $H_S\mathbf1=0$. We now use the normalized centered variance throughout, with $S=\operatorname{diag}(H_S/n_S,0)$. Expanding it retains the cross term involving labels; only the term $\lambda_1y_S^TH_Sy_S/(2n_S)$ is independent of the optimization variables. The explicit-feature counterpart therefore has $c=\lambda_1\Psi_S^TH_Sy_S/n_S$, which is retained in the corrected optimizer. There is no fixed residual-mean initialization or fix-then-freeze step.

% -------------Reviewer 3, Concern 3--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 3, Concern 3}}}
\emph{Please clarify the definition and derivation of the MMD-based domain adaptation term. In Eq.\ (4), it is presented as the standard distance between the source- and target-domain mean embeddings under a fixed RKHS mapping. When the kernel mapping is fixed, this formulation appears to be independent of the model parameters being optimized. However, Eq.\ (10) expresses it as a kernelized quadratic term involving the model coefficients, which appears to measure the difference between the mean predictions or projected means of the two domains. The authors should explain how Eq.\ (4) is transformed into Eq.\ (10) and clarify whether this term aligns the complete feature-space distributions or only constrains the difference between the two domains along the prediction direction.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We agree that the original two equations were inconsistent. With a fixed RKHS map, the standard squared mean-embedding distance $\lVert\bar\phi_S-\bar\phi_T\rVert_{\mathcal H}^2$ is constant with respect to the regressor and therefore cannot yield the coefficient-dependent quadratic term. We have replaced it throughout by the projected predictive-mean penalty $\frac{\lambda_2}{2}[\boldsymbol w^T(\bar\phi_S-\bar\phi_T)]^2$. If $\boldsymbol a$ is the signed source--target averaging vector and $\boldsymbol w=\Phi^T\boldsymbol\beta$, then $\boldsymbol w^T(\bar\phi_S-\bar\phi_T)=\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol K\boldsymbol a$, so its square is $\boldsymbol\beta^T\boldsymbol K\boldsymbol a\boldsymbol a^T\boldsymbol K\boldsymbol\beta$. The intercept cancels between domain means. This term constrains only the source--target difference along the learned prediction direction; it is not full feature-space distribution alignment and is no longer described as standard MMD.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Related Work'', subsection ``Transfer Learning and MMD'', near the revised passage:}\par

\begingroup\ResponseOriginalSafeOn\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
A fundamental challenge in transfer learning is measuring and reducing the distribution discrepancy. MMD is a widely used non-parametric metric that measures the distance between two distributions in an RKHS. Given source data $\{\boldsymbol{x}_{S,i}\}$ and target data $\{\boldsymbol{x}_{T,j}\}$, the squared MMD distance is defined as
\begin{equation}
\text{MMD}^2(D_S, D_T) = \left\| \frac{1}{n_S} \sum_{i=1}^{n_S} \phi(\boldsymbol{x}_{S,i}) - \frac{1}{n_T} \sum_{j=1}^{n_T} \phi(\boldsymbol{x}_{T,j}) \right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^2 ,
\end{equation}
where $\phi(\cdot)$ is the feature mapping induced by the kernel. By minimizing the MMD distance during training, the model learns a feature representation where the source and target domains are statistically aligned, enabling the classifier or regressor trained on the source domain to generalize well to the target domain. This alignment is particularly crucial for extreme-event forecasting, as it ensures that the learned predictor is robust to the feature-space shift between normal and extreme-event regimes.
\end{quote}
\endgroup\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}MMD measures a discrepancy between kernel mean embeddings. For a characteristic kernel, the population MMD is zero if and only if the two probability distributions coincide \citep{gretton2012kernel}. Its empirical squared mean-embedding discrepancy is}
\begin{equation*}
\color{blue}
\widehat{\operatorname{MMD}}^2(D_S,D_T)=\left\|\frac{1}{n_S}\sum_i\phi(\boldsymbol{x}_{S,i})-\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_j\phi(\boldsymbol{x}_{T,j})\right\|_{\mathcal H}^2.
\end{equation*}
{\color{blue}For fixed inputs and a fixed kernel map, this quantity does not depend on the predictor coefficients, so adding it to a regression objective cannot train those coefficients or learn a new representation. Our model instead penalizes the squared difference of mean predictions, $(\boldsymbol{w}^T(\bar\phi_S-\bar\phi_T))^2$. This can be viewed as empirical MMD with the linear kernel on scalar predictor outputs, rather than MMD in the original feature RKHS. It constrains one predictive direction; a zero value does not imply matching feature distributions or accurate target predictions. Domain alignment therefore provides a modeling motivation, not an unconditional transfer guarantee.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE related_mmd_scope
