% -------------Reviewer 3, Concern 4--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 3, Concern 4}}}
\emph{The mathematical basis of the proposed ``asymmetric variance regularization term'' should be clarified. The variance term in Eq.\ (4) is essentially based on squared centered residuals. Such a term penalizes positive and negative residuals in the same manner and does not explicitly depend on the quantile level. Therefore, its asymmetry and its essential difference from conventional symmetric variance regularization are not evident from the current formulation. The quantile-dependent asymmetry of the model appears to arise mainly from the pinball loss. If this is the case, the corresponding claims and descriptions of the variance regularization term should be revised accordingly.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
We agree that centered squared residuals penalize positive and negative residuals symmetrically and do not depend on the quantile level. The revised manuscript consistently calls this term symmetric centered source-residual variance regularization. Quantile-dependent asymmetry comes from the pinball loss. Translation invariance permits a nonzero residual mean but does not force a symmetric residual distribution, preserve a conditional quantile, or guarantee improved calibration. We removed the contradictory asymmetric-variance wording and do not claim that this penalty is a uniquely appropriate quantile modification.

The term is evaluated through the frozen matched analysis on all twelve tasks. For each task and seed, the Full-selected bandwidth, total loss mass, target fraction, rank, fitting rows, preprocessing, landmarks, and feature map are unchanged; the no-variance variant sets only $\lambda_1$ to zero. Within-site TL-QLDMR 18.090\% versus matched no-variance 17.870\%; cross-site stress TL-QLDMR 17.694\% versus matched no-variance 17.671\%. The Holm-significant TL-QLDMR-minus-no-variance effects were: Farm~1 (within-site): TL-QLDMR had lower squared error than No variance (MSE difference, TL-QLDMR minus No variance, $-0.292$ MW$^2$; 95\% block-bootstrap CI $[-0.524, -0.142]$, $p_{\mathrm{Holm}}=0.008$). These are conditional removal results under the TL-QLDMR-selected configuration; non-rejection does not establish equivalence. These findings are leakage-controlled reused-test evidence from a public-data period examined previously; they are not independent external confirmation. This is a conditional removal comparison, not an equivalence test or proof of a universally beneficial mechanism. The earlier common-setting Farm 6 comparison, in which the no-variance fit slightly lowers mean RMSE from 12.383799 to 12.352255 MW, remains only as supporting sensitivity evidence. The contribution claim is therefore limited to the specified combined formulation and its empirical evaluation.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised, added and removed the relevant text in Abstract, Section ``Introduction'', Section ``Introduction'', the closing roadmap paragraph, Section ``Related Work'', and the related passages listed below. The exact original wording and revised text are reproduced below at each approximate location.

% BEGIN VERIFIED CHANGE abstract
\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Abstract, near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
Accurate wind power forecasting under extreme events is critical for grid stability and renewable energy integration, yet remains a formidable challenge due to severe data scarcity and substantial distribution shifts between normal and extreme-event operating regimes. While kernel-based methods, particularly support vector regression and Large-margin Distribution Machine-based Regression (LDMR), have demonstrated strong performance in various regression tasks due to their theoretical guarantees and robustness on limited data, their application to extreme-event forecasting faces critical limitations: the i.i.d. assumption underlying standard kernel methods is fundamentally violated under cross-domain scenarios, and the symmetric variance minimization in LDMR implicitly encourages symmetric error distributions, which conflicts with the asymmetric nature of quantile-based interval prediction required for uncertainty quantification. To extend kernel-based regression to extreme-event forecasting, we propose Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR), which addresses these challenges through three synergistic innovations: (i) an asymmetric variance regularizer that preserves LDMR's distributional robustness while accommodating quantile-specific error asymmetry, (ii) a supervised transfer learning framework integrating maximum mean discrepancy for feature alignment and weighted pinball loss for label adaptation, enabling effective knowledge transfer from abundant normal-domain data to scarce extreme-event samples, and (iii) a scalable Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver reducing complexity from $O(N^3)$ to $O(T \cdot N \cdot m)$. Comprehensive experiments on six wind farms demonstrate that TL-QLDMR achieves competitive performance in both deterministic and probabilistic forecasting in the extreme-event domain, with superior reliability-sharpness trade-off and practical scalability, making it suitable for real-time applications where interpretability and theoretical guarantees are prioritized.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}Wind-power forecasting during meteorological extremes combines limited target labels with source--target distribution differences. We formulate the Transfer Learning Quantile Large-margin Distribution Machine for Regression (TL-QLDMR) using symmetric centered source-residual variance, a projected predictive-mean discrepancy, and weighted pinball loss. A frozen chronological comparison uses 128 target fitting labels and separates six primary within-site tasks from six secondary leave-one-farm-out stress tasks. In the primary within-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 13.913\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 18.090\%, ranked 3rd of six, and was outside the conservative first tier. In the secondary cross-site scope, histogram gradient boosting was the empirical winner for site-equal capacity-normalized root mean squared error at 14.923\%; TL-QLDMR achieved 17.694\%, ranked 5th of six, and remained in the conservative first tier. First-tier membership is non-rejection of inferiority rather than equivalence or superiority. Of 60 Holm-adjusted task comparisons, 1 favored TL-QLDMR and 4 favored a comparator. With its settings held fixed, TL-QLDMR ranked 2nd of four in the primary matched scope and 2nd of four in the secondary matched scope; 2 Holm-adjusted removal effects favored TL-QLDMR and 0 favored a removal variant. TL-QLDMR had the lowest mean task rank in both matched scopes. The matched effects are conditional because the variants were not independently retuned. The public Q3--Q4 period had been examined previously, so these results are test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation and do not establish universal model superiority.}
\end{quote}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Introduction'', near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
Against this backdrop, extending kernel-based methods from the normal-operating domain to the extreme-event domain introduces three critical challenges. First, the i.i.d. assumption is systematically violated when transferring knowledge from normal (source domain) to extreme-event (target domain) conditions. Recent wind-power studies have explored transfer learning and domain adaptation \citep{yin2021serioparallel, wang2024scarcity, dong2023mdan}; however, their principled integration with kernel-based regression remains open. Second, there exists a fundamental theoretical tension between LDMR's variance minimization, which implicitly encourages symmetric error distributions, and quantile regression at level $\tau \neq 0.5$, which requires inherently asymmetric residual distributions. Reconciling distributional robustness and quantile-specific asymmetry requires a principled modification of the LDMR framework. Third, existing transfer learning approaches for wind power forecasting predominantly adopt unsupervised adaptation strategies that underutilize scarce target-domain labels \citep{yin2021serioparallel, wang2024scarcity, dong2023mdan}. A more effective framework should leverage both feature-space alignment and label-space supervision, strategically weighting target samples to guide model adaptation.
\end{quote}

Against this backdrop, extending kernel-based methods from the normal-operating domain to the {\color{blue}meteorological-tail target domain} introduces three critical challenges. {\color{blue}First, the source and target distributions differ by their meteorological selection rules, while consecutive forecasting windows may also be dependent. These are separate obstacles to interpreting a pooled random-window score as performance on future extreme conditions.} Recent wind-power studies have explored transfer learning and domain adaptation \citep{yin2021serioparallel, wang2024scarcity, dong2023mdan}. {\color{blue}The setting studied here is narrower: a fixed kernel predictor, labeled target training windows, and a sample-level meteorological-tail domain. Second, residual-spread regularization and quantile estimation have different roles: the former penalizes dispersion, whereas the latter assigns different costs to underprediction and overprediction. A centered variance penalty does not impose residual symmetry or a zero residual mean. The methodological question is how to combine these terms consistently under source--target imbalance. Third, the present setting requires an explicit rule for using the limited target labels together with source observations. Here we examine a specified predictive-discrepancy penalty together with domain-weighted label supervision.}

\begingroup\ResponseOriginalSafeOn\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\subsection{LDMR}
While SVR and SVQR focus on maximizing the minimum margin, they largely ignore the statistical distribution of the margin over the entire dataset. LDMR was proposed to improve generalization by explicitly optimizing the distribution of the margins.
From early large-margin distribution formulations to least-squares and mode-seeking variants, LDMR has evolved into a practical framework for robust learning under noisy conditions \citep{zhang2014large, zhang2019optimal, gupta2021least, hazarika2023mode}.

The key idea of LDMR is to not only maximize the margin of the support vectors but also to minimize the variance of the error distribution for all samples. A typical LDMR formulation for regression integrates two additional statistical regularization terms into the objective function
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ldmr_concept}
\min_{\boldsymbol{w}, b} \frac{1}{2} \|\boldsymbol{w}\|^2 + \lambda_1 \text{Var}(\text{Residuals}) + \lambda_2 \text{Mean}(\text{Residuals}) + C \sum_{i=1}^{n} L(y_i, f(\boldsymbol{x}_i)),
\end{equation}
by constraining the variance, LDMR forces the prediction errors to be clustered tightly around zero, leading to a more compact and robust hypothesis space. However, this variance minimization implicitly encourages symmetric error distributions. Our work extends this concept by introducing an asymmetric variance regularization mechanism suitable for quantile regression, which preserves the distributional robustness of LDMR while accommodating the inherent asymmetry required for accurate quantile estimation.
\end{quote}
\endgroup\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\textbf{LDMR}
{\color{blue}The large-margin distribution machine introduced by \citet{zhang2014large} optimizes classification-margin statistics. Its minimum-margin motivation should not be transferred directly to regression: SVR regularizes function flatness while penalizing errors outside an $\epsilon$ tube, and SVQR combines norm regularization with pinball loss \citep{smola2004tutorial,takeuchi2006nonparametric}. \citet{rastogi2020ldmr} developed an LDM-inspired regression model whose objective combines $\epsilon$-insensitive and quadratic losses. The least-squares extension changes inequality constraints to equalities \citep{gupta2021least}, while \citet{hazarika2023mode} combines regression models with empirical mode decomposition and ensemble empirical mode decomposition for sediment-load prediction. The latter concerns signal decomposition, not mode-seeking estimation.}

{\color{blue}In the present formulation, residual dispersion is measured by the variance about the current source residual mean. This is a symmetric, translation-invariant penalty; it neither fixes that mean at zero nor prescribes residual symmetry or Gaussianity. Weighted pinball loss supplies the quantile-dependent costs. We therefore define and analyze the proposed objective explicitly rather than use a generic residual-mean-plus-variance expression as a representation of prior LDMR methods.}
\end{quote}
% END VERIFIED CHANGE related_variance

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Proposed Method'', subsection ``TL-QLDMR Model Formulation'', under the subheading ``Objective Function'', near the revised passage:}\par

\begingroup\ResponseOriginalSafeOn\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
    \item \textbf{Distribution Variance}: This term is the core of our proposed Quantile LDMR model, incorporating a critical modification to the original LDMR variance.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textbf{Theoretical Conflict}: The original LDMR minimizes the variance of residuals, which implicitly encourages a symmetric, concentrated error distribution around zero. However, quantile regression at level $\tau \neq 0.5$ requires an asymmetric residual distribution where approximately $\tau$ proportion of errors are negative. Applying a symmetric variance penalty would force the residual distribution towards symmetry, degrading the skewness required for accurate quantile estimation.
        \item \textbf{Asymmetric Modification}: To resolve this, we employ an asymmetric variance regularization based on the algebraic residuals. This design allows the model to reduce error dispersion without constraining the distribution's direction, thereby preserving the non-symmetric properties essential for the Pinball Loss and improving interval coverage.
    \end{itemize}
\end{quote}
\endgroup\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\begin{itemize}
    \item {\color{blue}\textbf{Residual-Variance Regularization}: The source-only term is a symmetric penalty on centered residuals and contains no quantile parameter. For any residual vector $\boldsymbol{u}$ and scalar $a$, $\|\boldsymbol{H}_S(\boldsymbol{u}+a\boldsymbol{1})\|^2=\|\boldsymbol{H}_S\boldsymbol{u}\|^2$. It controls dispersion without fixing the residual mean or imposing a distributional shape. Quantile dependence enters through pinball loss. Translation invariance alone does not ensure that the penalized population minimizer equals the target conditional quantile; no such consistency or calibration guarantee is asserted.}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\small
\subsection{Experiment 4: Ablation Study}\label{sec:exp4}

To validate the contribution of the three core components (transfer learning, LDMR variance regularization, and MMD feature alignment), this ablation experiment evaluates structurally reduced variants on both point and interval tasks. Additionally, to verify the necessity of asymmetric variance regularization for quantile regression, we include LDMR-Quantile (SymVar), which replaces the asymmetric variance term with standard symmetric variance minimization while retaining the transfer learning framework.

The full TL-QLDMR framework is compared against four architectural reductions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{LDMR-Quantile (SymVar)}: Replaces asymmetric variance regularization with symmetric variance minimization, testing whether the asymmetry is necessary for quantile-specific calibration.
    \item \textbf{w/o Transfer (Target-only quantile LDMR, QLDMR)}: Trained exclusively on extreme-event target samples without source-domain integration or MMD alignment.
    \item \textbf{w/o LDMR (Variance Penalty)}: The asymmetric variance regularizer is removed, deteriorating the framework into a generalized Transfer SVR/SVQR variant that lacks distributional robustness.
    \item \textbf{w/o MMD (Feature Alignment)}: The algorithm employs cross-domain training data but disables MMD alignment, relying purely on weighted objective loss.
\end{enumerate}

Table~\ref{tab:ablation_results} reports the ablation results on Farm~6. The full TL-QLDMR consistently attains the best deterministic and probabilistic performance, indicating that all three components contribute non-trivially to final accuracy and calibration quality.

\begin{table*}[ht]

Model Variants & RMSE & $R^2$ & PICP & MPIW & PINAW & CWC \\
\midrule
w/o LDMR (Variance)     & 8.205 & 0.9461 & 0.949 & 25.925 & 0.2697 & 0.3507 \\
w/o Transfer            & 7.930 & 0.9497 & 0.952 & 26.891 & 0.2797 & 0.2797 \\
LDMR-Quantile (SymVar)  & 7.868 & 0.9472 & 0.952 & 29.114 & 0.3029 & 0.3029 \\
w/o MMD                 & 7.745 & 0.9520 & 0.947 & 26.049 & 0.2710 & 0.3528 \\
\textbf{TL-QLDMR (Full)} & \textbf{7.476} & \textbf{0.9557} & \textbf{0.959} & \textbf{25.791} & \textbf{0.2683} & \textbf{0.2683} \\

\begin{center}
\captionsetup{type=figure,hypcap=false}
\includegraphics[width=0.82\linewidth]{experiment4/plots/residual_distribution.png}
\captionof{figure}{Residual density comparison between TL-QLDMR and ablated variants on the Farm~6 test set.}
\label{fig:ablation_residual}
\end{center}

The ablation outcomes confirm that each component contributes materially to robustness. Removing transfer learning reduces both point accuracy ($R^2$: 0.9557 $\rightarrow$ 0.9497) and interval quality (CWC: 0.2683 $\rightarrow$ 0.2797), indicating that target-only training is insufficient under strong domain shift. Removing LDMR regularization or MMD alignment causes clear interval-quality degradation (CWC rises to 0.3507 and 0.3528), even when point-metric changes are smaller, showing that residual-shape control and feature alignment are central to reliable uncertainty estimation.

Critically, the LDMR-Quantile (SymVar) variant, which replaces asymmetric variance with symmetric variance minimization, exhibits degraded performance on both point prediction (RMSE: 7.868 vs. 7.476) and interval prediction (CWC: 0.3029 vs. 0.2683, PINAW: 0.3029 vs. 0.2683). This degradation empirically validates our theoretical analysis in Section~\ref{novel}: symmetric variance minimization, while effective for mean regression, conflicts with the asymmetric residual distribution required for accurate quantile estimation. The symmetric regularizer forces errors toward a centered, Gaussian-like distribution, thereby degrading interval calibration at non-median quantiles.

The residual-density comparison in Fig.~\ref{fig:ablation_residual} supports this conclusion by showing tighter central concentration and weaker heavy tails for the full TL-QLDMR model; some ablated variants exhibit sharper central peaks but noticeably thicker tails, which corresponds to a higher probability of large-error events.

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Introduction'', near the revised passage:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
At the methodological level, a fundamental limitation shared by both SVR and SVQR is that they optimize only the minimum margin while ignoring the statistical distribution of margins across the entire dataset. To overcome this limitation, the Large-margin Distribution Machine-based Regression (LDMR) paradigm was introduced, which explicitly optimizes both the mean and variance of the margin distribution \citep{zhang2019optimal, gupta2021least}. By concentrating prediction errors tightly around zero, LDMR achieves superior generalization compared to classical SVR on a wide range of regression tasks \citep{gupta2021least, hazarika2023mode}. However, LDMR has not been systematically applied to wind power forecasting, particularly under extreme-event conditions where both distributional robustness and probabilistic interval prediction are required. These characteristics make it a promising candidate for extension to forecasting in the extreme-event domain.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}SVR combines norm regularization with an $\epsilon$-insensitive loss, whereas support vector quantile regression uses a quantile-dependent pinball loss \citep{smola2004tutorial,takeuchi2006nonparametric}. The original large-margin distribution machine concerns classification margins \citep{zhang2014large}; its regression extension, LDMR, combines $\epsilon$-insensitive and quadratic losses \citep{rastogi2020ldmr}. Later work includes a least-squares formulation and applications with empirical mode decomposition \citep{gupta2021least,hazarika2023mode}. These developments motivate examining residual dispersion together with quantile loss in supervised transfer. Our centered residual-variance term is specified separately below; it is not identified with every earlier LDMR objective or with a mechanism that forces residuals to be symmetric.}
\end{quote}

Therefore, the scalable solver preserves the same four components as the exact formulation: structural risk, source-domain variance regularization, MMD-based alignment, and weighted pinball loss. \noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The same $1/n_S$ normalization appears in both $\boldsymbol{R}$ and $\boldsymbol{c}$ because they arise from a single expansion of the centered source-residual penalty. Omitting $\boldsymbol{c}$ would instead penalize the spread of predictions and would define a different model. Relative to the exact formulation, only the kernel representation is approximated; the residual-variance normalization and loss-sum convention are preserved.}


{\color{blue}\textbf{Relation to weighted SVQR.} For a fixed feature map, $\boldsymbol{R}\succeq\boldsymbol{I}$. Set $\boldsymbol{w}_0=\boldsymbol{R}^{-1}\boldsymbol{c}$, $\boldsymbol{v}=\boldsymbol{R}^{1/2}(\boldsymbol{w}-\boldsymbol{w}_0)$, $\widetilde\psi(\boldsymbol{x})=\boldsymbol{R}^{-1/2}\psi(\boldsymbol{x})$, and $\widetilde y_k=y_k-\psi(\boldsymbol{x}_k)^T\boldsymbol{w}_0$. Completing the square makes Eq.~(20) equivalent, up to an additive constant, to
\begin{equation*}
\min_{\boldsymbol{v},b}\ \frac12\|\boldsymbol{v}\|^2+\sum_k C_k L_\tau\bigl(\widetilde y_k,\boldsymbol{v}^T\widetilde\psi(\boldsymbol{x}_k)+b\bigr).
\end{equation*}
Thus the objective is a weighted SVQR problem with a data-dependent feature transformation and label shift \citep{takeuchi2006nonparametric}. When $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0$, it reduces to weighted SVQR in the original fixed features. The centered source-residual term contributes both a covariance-dependent quadratic term and a label-dependent linear term; the projected discrepancy adds a positive-semidefinite term of rank at most one. This identifies the precise modification to the established objective, rather than a new asymmetric loss or a new class of optimizers. It does not establish that the combination is uniquely preferable or improves target prediction.}


{\color{blue}Unregularized expected pinball risk is minimized by a conditional quantile \citep{takeuchi2006nonparametric}. Additional penalties and source--target weighting can change that minimizer. An unregularized intercept yields weighted empirical sign-count inequalities at an exact optimum, but these pooled training conditions do not imply conditional or target-only calibration. Finite-epoch Adam is not asserted to satisfy exact optimality conditions.}
\end{quote}

{\color{blue}The experiments use the supplied original workbooks with chronological separation of fitting, validation, calibration, and testing. Model fitting uses 1 January--31 December 2019. The first quarter of 2020 is the validation period: the independently tuned formal procedure comparison uses Q1 only for its frozen model-selection protocol, whereas the fixed-setting sensitivity analyses that follow do not use Q1 to select their common reference configuration. April--June 2020 (Q2) supplies interval-calibration labels for the procedure comparison, and July--December 2020 (Q3--Q4) supplies test labels. The procedure-comparison workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after its selection and analysis specifications are locked. The matched point analysis uses no Q2 label, and its configurations and analysis specification are locked before its Q3--Q4 evaluation. All boundaries are left-inclusive and right-exclusive at midnight. The forecast horizon is 15 minutes: each input contains the preceding 24 observations, with consecutive input-to-input and last-input-to-target intervals of exactly 15 minutes. Adjacent windows on opposite sides of a period boundary may share already observed input rows, as in rolling forecasting, but every forecast target belongs to exactly one period. No Q1, Q2, or Q3--Q4 label enters the 2019 fit; no Q2 or Q3--Q4 label enters Q1 model selection; and no Q3--Q4 label enters fixed Q2 calibration. Past-only rolling calibration is evaluated separately: it can use Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed strictly before the current forecast and adds the current outcome only after issuing that forecast. Random sampling is confined to the 2019 fitting pool and to algorithmic landmark seeds; it does not create the calendar partitions.}

{\color{blue}The study uses two common meteorological input tracks across all six sites. The formal validation-selected comparison uses four wind speeds, temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sine/cosine encodings of four wind directions at each of the 24 strictly preceding observations, giving 15 variables per step and 360 flattened inputs. The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses retain the earlier track of four wind speeds, temperature, and the same eight directional encodings, giving 13 variables per step and 312 flattened inputs. Neither track uses past power or future meteorological values. Times written as 24:00 are normalized to the next day; all rows sharing an ambiguous duplicate timestamp are removed before chronological sorting. Missing codes ($-99$), nonfinite values, all-zero meteorological records, negative wind speeds, and directions outside $[0,360]$ are treated as missing covariates. Targets with missing power, hub wind, or temperature and windows with non-15-minute gaps are excluded by fixed rules. Other power values, including negative or above-capacity observations, are retained. Missing input values are replaced by lag-specific fitting means; an entirely missing coordinate uses zero. Feature standardization and capacity-normalized label standardization use only the observations actually fitted in that branch, excluding unused target labels in scarcity experiments. No future-value filling, clipping, or error-based exclusions are applied. The original files are preserved, although their upstream measurement and processing history is not fully documented.}

{\color{blue}Domain thresholds use valid meteorological observations from 2019 only. Farm~6 thresholds are 15.43\,m/s for wind and 10.24/31.36\,$^\circ$C for temperature; its training set contains 32,832 source and 2,076 target windows. Table~6 reports all six sites. Test membership is determined retrospectively from observed target-time weather; this protocol does not forecast event onset. The time split, missing-value rules, and common-setting comparison grids were specified before those fits. This is a temporal holdout within a previously studied public dataset.}

{\color{blue}The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses use $\lambda_1=\lambda_2=1$, RBF bandwidth parameter $\gamma=0.003$, 256 requested landmarks, batch size 256, Adam learning rate 0.01, and 64 epochs, on an Intel Xeon Platinum 8452Y host with one computational thread (Python 3.10.9, NumPy 2.2.6, and scikit-learn 1.7.2). These values define a common reference configuration for probing model behavior; the formal comparison applies its separately frozen Q1 selection protocol. Unless varied explicitly, loss coefficients are $C_S=1000/(2n_S)$ and $C_T=1000/(2n_T)$, so both domains receive equal total coefficient mass and $n_SC_S+n_TC_T=1000$. Target-only fitting uses $C_T=1000/n_T$, centered target residual variance, no projected discrepancy, and its own fitting statistics and landmarks. Its epochs are raised to the smallest integer giving at least as many Adam updates as the paired full model; equal update opportunities do not certify equal optimization accuracy. The full, no-variance, no-discrepancy, and target-only variants use seeds 0, 1, and 2. These are algorithmic repeats on a shared test period, not independent datasets or confidence intervals.}

{\color{blue}Point prediction uses $\tau=0.5$. Interval fits use $\tau_L=0.025$ and $\tau_U=0.975$. Define ordered endpoints $\ell(x)=\min\{f_{\tau_L}(x),f_{\tau_U}(x)\}$ and $u(x)=\max\{f_{\tau_L}(x),f_{\tau_U}(x)\}$. Calibration scores are $s_i=\max\{\ell(x_i)-y_i,y_i-u(x_i),0\}$. With $\alpha=0.05$, set $k=\lceil(n_{\rm cal}+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$, $q=s_{(k)}$, and report $[\ell(x)-q,u(x)+q]$. A finite interval requires $k\le n_{\rm cal}$. On Farm~6, $n_{\rm cal}=225$ and $k=215$. This formula defines the fixed Q2 expansion, to which no Q3--Q4 label contributes. The separately reported past-only rolling expansion may use only Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed before each forecast; it never uses the current or a future outcome. % -------------Reviewer 3, Concern 5--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 3, Concern 5}}}
\emph{The manuscript assigns a substantially larger penalty weight to the target domain than to the source domain in order to prevent the large number of source-domain samples from dominating joint training. However, the current objective function directly sums the losses from the two domains. Their relative contributions therefore depend not only on the selected penalty weights but also on the corresponding sample sizes. For example, for Farm 6, the source domain contains 66,009 samples, whereas the target domain contains 4,144 samples, resulting in an approximate sample-size ratio of 16 to 1. At the same time, the candidate target-domain penalty weights are much larger than the candidate source-domain weights, resulting in a per-sample weight ratio ranging from 250 to 20,000. Therefore, this setting may not merely compensate for sample imbalance but may cause the optimization to be dominated by the target-domain loss. The existing ``w/o Transfer'' and ``w/o MMD'' ablation studies cannot independently identify the contribution of this weighting mechanism. The authors are encouraged to report the final source- and target-domain penalty weights used in each experiment and conduct a sensitivity analysis of the weighting strategy. Possible comparisons could include equal weighting, domain-size-normalized weighting, sample-imbalance-based weighting, and the current strategy.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
The reviewer is correct that summed losses are governed by coefficient mass: the target/source contribution ratio is $n_TC_T/(n_SC_S)$, not simply $C_T/C_S$. The revised notation therefore parameterizes the loss through total mass $A=n_SC_S+n_TC_T$ and target fraction $p=n_TC_T/A$, so $C_S=A(1-p)/n_S$ and $C_T=Ap/n_T$. The existing controlled Farm 6 sensitivity analysis keeps $A=1000$ and compares equal per-sample weights, equal domain masses, target mass ten times source mass, and the historical per-sample ratio rescaled to the same total. Their seed-0 point RMSE values are 12.102063, 12.336268, 12.660232, and 12.662003 MW, respectively. The corresponding calibrated interval PICP/mean-width pairs are 0.986117/56.701425, 0.976265/48.988181, 0.974474/42.757565, and 0.965069/39.768748 MW. This is an accuracy--width trade-off, not evidence that the target-heavy allocation is optimal.

In the formal v2 comparison, the kernel procedures select $A$ and $p$ on Q1 within the same 54-query budget provided to every procedure; HistGBR uses its method-specific tree and target-weight coordinates under the same query count. The appendix reports the locked values and validation scores for every task and procedure. The locked appendix reports the selected total loss mass $A$ and target mass fraction $p$ for all 60 kernel task--method pairs; target-only support-vector quantile regression has $p=1$, while the tree comparator reports its separate target-weight coordinate. Every free coordinate was selected on Q1 within the common 54-query budget before Q2 calibration or Q3--Q4 evaluation, so no held-out outcome was used to favor a source--target weighting. The frozen matched ablation then holds both $A$ and $p$, together with all rows, preprocessing, landmarks, feature maps, ranks, and other hyperparameters, fixed while only $\lambda_1$ and/or $\lambda_2$ are removed. Thus the matched component comparison cannot attribute an effect to a simultaneous change in source/target weighting, while the separately tuned procedure comparison remains a comparison of complete selection pipelines.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised, added, and removed the relevant text in Sections ``Proposed Method'' and ``Experiments''. The exact original wording and revised text are reproduced below at each approximate location.

{\color{blue}The experiments use the supplied original workbooks with chronological separation of fitting, validation, calibration, and testing. Model fitting uses 1 January--31 December 2019. The first quarter of 2020 is the validation period: the independently tuned formal procedure comparison uses Q1 only for its frozen model-selection protocol, whereas the fixed-setting sensitivity analyses that follow do not use Q1 to select their common reference configuration. April--June 2020 (Q2) supplies interval-calibration labels for the procedure comparison, and July--December 2020 (Q3--Q4) supplies test labels. The procedure-comparison workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after its selection and analysis specifications are locked. The matched point analysis uses no Q2 label, and its configurations and analysis specification are locked before its Q3--Q4 evaluation. All boundaries are left-inclusive and right-exclusive at midnight. The forecast horizon is 15 minutes: each input contains the preceding 24 observations, with consecutive input-to-input and last-input-to-target intervals of exactly 15 minutes. Adjacent windows on opposite sides of a period boundary may share already observed input rows, as in rolling forecasting, but every forecast target belongs to exactly one period. No Q1, Q2, or Q3--Q4 label enters the 2019 fit; no Q2 or Q3--Q4 label enters Q1 model selection; and no Q3--Q4 label enters fixed Q2 calibration. Past-only rolling calibration is evaluated separately: it can use Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed strictly before the current forecast and adds the current outcome only after issuing that forecast. Random sampling is confined to the 2019 fitting pool and to algorithmic landmark seeds; it does not create the calendar partitions.}

{\color{blue}The study uses two common meteorological input tracks across all six sites. The formal validation-selected comparison uses four wind speeds, temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sine/cosine encodings of four wind directions at each of the 24 strictly preceding observations, giving 15 variables per step and 360 flattened inputs. The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses retain the earlier track of four wind speeds, temperature, and the same eight directional encodings, giving 13 variables per step and 312 flattened inputs. Neither track uses past power or future meteorological values. Times written as 24:00 are normalized to the next day; all rows sharing an ambiguous duplicate timestamp are removed before chronological sorting. Missing codes ($-99$), nonfinite values, all-zero meteorological records, negative wind speeds, and directions outside $[0,360]$ are treated as missing covariates. Targets with missing power, hub wind, or temperature and windows with non-15-minute gaps are excluded by fixed rules. Other power values, including negative or above-capacity observations, are retained. Missing input values are replaced by lag-specific fitting means; an entirely missing coordinate uses zero. Feature standardization and capacity-normalized label standardization use only the observations actually fitted in that branch, excluding unused target labels in scarcity experiments. No future-value filling, clipping, or error-based exclusions are applied. The original files are preserved, although their upstream measurement and processing history is not fully documented.}

{\color{blue}Domain thresholds use valid meteorological observations from 2019 only. Farm~6 thresholds are 15.43\,m/s for wind and 10.24/31.36\,$^\circ$C for temperature; its training set contains 32,832 source and 2,076 target windows. Table~6 reports all six sites. Test membership is determined retrospectively from observed target-time weather; this protocol does not forecast event onset. The time split, missing-value rules, and common-setting comparison grids were specified before those fits. This is a temporal holdout within a previously studied public dataset.}

The Nystr\"{o}m-SGD solver is tuned over landmark size $m \in [800, 1500]$, learning rate in $\{0.005, 0.01\}$, and training epochs in $[48, 80]$, with mini-batch size fixed at 256. \noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
\par\noindent\textbf{Validation-selected predictive comparison}\par
{\color{blue}We compare TL-QLDMR, its no-variance and no-discrepancy variants, pooled weighted support vector quantile regression (SVQR), target-only SVQR, and histogram gradient boosting with quantile loss (HistGBR). The six within-site normal-to-extreme tasks form the primary scope, and the six leave-one-farm-out tasks form a secondary transfer-stress scope. Every site and method is retained in its prespecified scope. Within each primary task, the source observations are normal-domain windows from the target farm; within each secondary task, normal-domain source observations come from the other five farms.}

{\color{blue}Each task uses exactly 128 extreme-domain target fitting labels selected deterministically from 2019. The cells are training month crossed with mutually exclusive cold, hot, and high-wind/cut-out categories, assigned in that priority order from target-time meteorological covariates within the fitting period only; power values are not used in acquisition. Each nonempty cell first receives one observation; the remaining labels are allocated by the largest-remainder rule in proportion to the cells' remaining capacities, and observations within a cell are chosen near equally spaced clock-time targets. A primary task uses at most 7,500 normal-domain source windows from the same farm, deterministically thinned in chronological order, whereas a secondary task uses at most 1,500 normal-domain source windows from each of the other five farms. The 128 labels are the model-fitting budget rather than the total target supervision. For Farms~1--6, the additional target-domain Q1 selection counts are 169, 617, 2,410, 212, 134, and 177, and the Q2 calibration counts are 305, 102, 862, 319, 362, and 225, respectively.}

{\color{blue}The formal-comparison input at each forecast contains four wind-speed measurements, sine and cosine encodings of four wind-direction measurements, temperature, atmospheric pressure, and relative humidity at each of the 24 strictly preceding 15-minute observations, giving 360 flattened meteorological inputs. Past power and future meteorological values are excluded. Power labels are divided by their farm-specific nominal capacity before fit-only label standardization and are mapped back to the target farm's MW scale for evaluation. Missing-value imputation and feature and label standardization are fitted only on the 2019 model-fitting rows. For pooled models, the source and target domains each contribute one half of the preprocessing weight; target-only preprocessing uses only its target fitting rows. Nystr\"om landmarks are constructed without labels from fitting inputs. A pooled landmark pool contains at most 2,000 source and 2,000 target rows and assigns total K-means weight one half to each domain; target-only construction uses only target fitting rows. K-means is used when the requested rank is smaller than the pool, while all pool rows are retained when the requested rank equals the pool size; any resulting effective-rank cap is recorded.}

{\color{blue}For each task--method pair, the frozen search rule issues 54 effective Q1 configuration queries through three predeclared sequential stages of 18 new queries: a base search, a middle active-regularizer search or method-equivalent refinement, and a local joint refinement. The middle stage either varies the active regularizer coefficients while retaining the base incumbent's other coordinates or applies a method-equivalent deterministic refinement around that incumbent; the joint stage is generated locally around the incumbent retained after the middle stage. Within a task--method pair, the 18 effective configurations in each stage are distinct from one another and from every earlier-stage query, giving 54 distinct effective queries across the three stages. Kernel candidates are scored by the mean target-Q1 RMSE of the $\tau=0.5$ fit across seeds 0, 1, and 2, whereas deterministic HistGBR is fitted once at seed 0 per query. The pooled kernel searches include requested Nystr\"om ranks 128, 256, and 512, and target-only SVQR uses ranks 32, 64, and 128. Inactive hyperparameter coordinates are ignored when effective-query uniqueness is checked. Equal query counts provide a common configuration-query budget; they do not imply equal model capacity, numbers of solver attempts, wall-clock cost, or exhaustive optimization.}

{\color{blue}Candidate generation, model fitting, preprocessing, landmark construction, and Q1 scoring are completed before the immutable selection lock is created, and the analysis specification is separately frozen before any formal-comparison Q3--Q4 output is read. Each locked configuration is refitted on the unchanged 2019 fitting rows; Q1 labels are not added to the fit. Q2 is reserved for interval calibration, and the formal workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after the selection and analysis locks and then evaluates it under the locked settings. Kernel settings use landmark seeds 0, 1, and 2, and deterministic HistGBR uses seed 0. No task, method, seed, or configuration is selected from Q2 or Q3--Q4 performance. Because the public-data test period had already been examined in earlier work, this design provides test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation.}

{\color{blue}Every kernel fit is first attempted for at most 3,000 ADMM iterations. The numerical certificate is checked every 25 iterations and requires $P-D\leq 10^{-7}+10^{-3}\max\{1,|P|,|D|\}$. If the first attempt misses this condition, a second attempt is warm-started from its returned best-primal $(\boldsymbol{w},b)$ incumbent, with freshly initialized split and dual states, and is allowed at most 12,000 additional ADMM iterations; the data, feature map, objective, and hyperparameters remain unchanged. The candidate remains in the audit record but is ineligible for selection if any required selection seed still misses the certificate. Under the original execution rule, a locked main-study or matched-ablation fit that still missed the certificate produced no retained result. This is a numerical primal--dual-gap certificate for the chosen fixed-feature objective, not an interval-arithmetic proof, a certificate of Nystr\"om approximation error, or a predictive-generalization guarantee.}

{\color{blue}One locked main-study fit exhausted these two attempts with a relative gap of 0.0010217, compared with the unchanged 0.001 tolerance. Before its Q3--Q4 predictive scores were inspected, we froze a performance-blind solver amendment that committed the hashes of all then-existing completion artifacts and the already frozen analysis specifications. For an otherwise exact locked main or matched fit with no completed result, the amendment permitted one further warm restart, from the same best-primal incumbent and fresh split and dual states, for at most 96,000 iterations under the same objective, data, feature map, hyperparameters, and certificate tolerance. No completed result could be replaced. The single triggering main-study fit then met the unchanged certificate; no matched-ablation fit required the amendment. Selection, calibration, prediction, and analysis rules were unchanged, and the original failed record, model, amendment lock, and completion sidecars are retained in the reproducibility package.}
\end{quote}

% -------------Reviewer 3, Concern 6--------------
\textcolor{customgreen}{
\subsubsection*{\underline{\textbf{Reviewer 3, Concern 6}}}
\emph{Please provide further details on how the training, validation, and test sets were constructed. Section 4.3 states that the data were randomly divided using a fixed random seed, while Figure 1 shows that the input samples were generated using sliding windows of length 24. Please clarify whether the datasets were divided chronologically, by independent time periods, or by randomly splitting the window samples. If overlapping windows can appear in different subsets, the authors should also explain how potential temporal information leakage was avoided.}
}\\

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author response}}}
The revised manuscript gives explicit chronological boundaries. Forecast targets in 2019 supply fitting data, 2020 Q1 supplies validation labels, Q2 supplies interval-calibration labels, and Q3--Q4 supplies locked test labels. Every target is predicted from the 24 strictly preceding 15-minute observations. Consecutive windows, including those adjacent to a period boundary, may share already observed input rows, as in rolling forecasting, but no target row belongs to more than one period and no future label is used as an input, imputation value, or selection signal. Ambiguous duplicate timestamps and windows containing a non-15-minute gap are removed by fixed rules. Imputation and standardization use only the fitting rows for the relevant branch, and random sampling is confined to the 2019 fitting pool and algorithmic landmark construction.

We also distinguish the two input tracks. The earlier fixed-setting sensitivity analyses use thirteen meteorological variables over 24 past lags, giving 312 inputs. The formal v2 comparison adds pressure and humidity and uses fifteen variables over the same 24 strictly preceding lags, giving 360 inputs. Neither track uses past power or future meteorological values. V2 deterministically selects 128 target fitting labels from 2019; Q1 and Q2 labels are additional and are reported separately rather than counted as fitting labels. The configuration lock is created before Q2 calibration and Q3--Q4 evaluation.

\color{black}
\subsubsection*{\textbf{\underline{Author action}}}
We revised the sampling description and added a detailed chronological construction paragraph covering overlapping histories, target separation, preprocessing, and missing or irregular timestamps.

\begin{quote}
\small
\par\noindent\textbf{Validation-selected predictive comparison}\par
{\color{blue}We compare TL-QLDMR, its no-variance and no-discrepancy variants, pooled weighted support vector quantile regression (SVQR), target-only SVQR, and histogram gradient boosting with quantile loss (HistGBR). The six within-site normal-to-extreme tasks form the primary scope, and the six leave-one-farm-out tasks form a secondary transfer-stress scope. Every site and method is retained in its prespecified scope. Within each primary task, the source observations are normal-domain windows from the target farm; within each secondary task, normal-domain source observations come from the other five farms.}

{\color{blue}Each task uses exactly 128 extreme-domain target fitting labels selected deterministically from 2019. The cells are training month crossed with mutually exclusive cold, hot, and high-wind/cut-out categories, assigned in that priority order from target-time meteorological covariates within the fitting period only; power values are not used in acquisition. Each nonempty cell first receives one observation; the remaining labels are allocated by the largest-remainder rule in proportion to the cells' remaining capacities, and observations within a cell are chosen near equally spaced clock-time targets. A primary task uses at most 7,500 normal-domain source windows from the same farm, deterministically thinned in chronological order, whereas a secondary task uses at most 1,500 normal-domain source windows from each of the other five farms. The 128 labels are the model-fitting budget rather than the total target supervision. For Farms~1--6, the additional target-domain Q1 selection counts are 169, 617, 2,410, 212, 134, and 177, and the Q2 calibration counts are 305, 102, 862, 319, 362, and 225, respectively.}

{\color{blue}The formal-comparison input at each forecast contains four wind-speed measurements, sine and cosine encodings of four wind-direction measurements, temperature, atmospheric pressure, and relative humidity at each of the 24 strictly preceding 15-minute observations, giving 360 flattened meteorological inputs. Past power and future meteorological values are excluded. Power labels are divided by their farm-specific nominal capacity before fit-only label standardization and are mapped back to the target farm's MW scale for evaluation. Missing-value imputation and feature and label standardization are fitted only on the 2019 model-fitting rows. For pooled models, the source and target domains each contribute one half of the preprocessing weight; target-only preprocessing uses only its target fitting rows. Nystr\"om landmarks are constructed without labels from fitting inputs. A pooled landmark pool contains at most 2,000 source and 2,000 target rows and assigns total K-means weight one half to each domain; target-only construction uses only target fitting rows. K-means is used when the requested rank is smaller than the pool, while all pool rows are retained when the requested rank equals the pool size; any resulting effective-rank cap is recorded.}

{\color{blue}For each task--method pair, the frozen search rule issues 54 effective Q1 configuration queries through three predeclared sequential stages of 18 new queries: a base search, a middle active-regularizer search or method-equivalent refinement, and a local joint refinement. The middle stage either varies the active regularizer coefficients while retaining the base incumbent's other coordinates or applies a method-equivalent deterministic refinement around that incumbent; the joint stage is generated locally around the incumbent retained after the middle stage. Within a task--method pair, the 18 effective configurations in each stage are distinct from one another and from every earlier-stage query, giving 54 distinct effective queries across the three stages. Kernel candidates are scored by the mean target-Q1 RMSE of the $\tau=0.5$ fit across seeds 0, 1, and 2, whereas deterministic HistGBR is fitted once at seed 0 per query. The pooled kernel searches include requested Nystr\"om ranks 128, 256, and 512, and target-only SVQR uses ranks 32, 64, and 128. Inactive hyperparameter coordinates are ignored when effective-query uniqueness is checked. Equal query counts provide a common configuration-query budget; they do not imply equal model capacity, numbers of solver attempts, wall-clock cost, or exhaustive optimization.}

{\color{blue}Candidate generation, model fitting, preprocessing, landmark construction, and Q1 scoring are completed before the immutable selection lock is created, and the analysis specification is separately frozen before any formal-comparison Q3--Q4 output is read. Each locked configuration is refitted on the unchanged 2019 fitting rows; Q1 labels are not added to the fit. Q2 is reserved for interval calibration, and the formal workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after the selection and analysis locks and then evaluates it under the locked settings. Kernel settings use landmark seeds 0, 1, and 2, and deterministic HistGBR uses seed 0. No task, method, seed, or configuration is selected from Q2 or Q3--Q4 performance. Because the public-data test period had already been examined in earlier work, this design provides test-locked evidence on a reused period rather than independent external confirmation.}

{\color{blue}Every kernel fit is first attempted for at most 3,000 ADMM iterations. The numerical certificate is checked every 25 iterations and requires $P-D\leq 10^{-7}+10^{-3}\max\{1,|P|,|D|\}$. If the first attempt misses this condition, a second attempt is warm-started from its returned best-primal $(\boldsymbol{w},b)$ incumbent, with freshly initialized split and dual states, and is allowed at most 12,000 additional ADMM iterations; the data, feature map, objective, and hyperparameters remain unchanged. The candidate remains in the audit record but is ineligible for selection if any required selection seed still misses the certificate. Under the original execution rule, a locked main-study or matched-ablation fit that still missed the certificate produced no retained result. This is a numerical primal--dual-gap certificate for the chosen fixed-feature objective, not an interval-arithmetic proof, a certificate of Nystr\"om approximation error, or a predictive-generalization guarantee.}

{\color{blue}One locked main-study fit exhausted these two attempts with a relative gap of 0.0010217, compared with the unchanged 0.001 tolerance. Before its Q3--Q4 predictive scores were inspected, we froze a performance-blind solver amendment that committed the hashes of all then-existing completion artifacts and the already frozen analysis specifications. For an otherwise exact locked main or matched fit with no completed result, the amendment permitted one further warm restart, from the same best-primal incumbent and fresh split and dual states, for at most 96,000 iterations under the same objective, data, feature map, hyperparameters, and certificate tolerance. No completed result could be replaced. The single triggering main-study fit then met the unchanged certificate; no matched-ablation fit required the amendment. Selection, calibration, prediction, and analysis rules were unchanged, and the original failed record, model, amendment lock, and completion sidecars are retained in the reproducibility package.}
\end{quote}

\noindent\textbf{$\blacktriangleright\blacktriangleright$ Section ``Experiments'', subsection ``Chronological protocol'', the opening paragraphs:}\par

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Original text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
No corresponding passage appears in the original manuscript. The following text is added in the chronological evaluation subsection of the revised manuscript.
\end{quote}

\noindent$\longrightarrow$\enspace\textbf{Revised text:}\par
\begin{quote}
\small
{\color{blue}The experiments use the supplied original workbooks with chronological separation of fitting, validation, calibration, and testing. Model fitting uses 1 January--31 December 2019. The first quarter of 2020 is the validation period: the independently tuned formal procedure comparison uses Q1 only for its frozen model-selection protocol, whereas the fixed-setting sensitivity analyses that follow do not use Q1 to select their common reference configuration. April--June 2020 (Q2) supplies interval-calibration labels for the procedure comparison, and July--December 2020 (Q3--Q4) supplies test labels. The procedure-comparison workflow accesses Q3--Q4 only after its selection and analysis specifications are locked. The matched point analysis uses no Q2 label, and its configurations and analysis specification are locked before its Q3--Q4 evaluation. All boundaries are left-inclusive and right-exclusive at midnight. The forecast horizon is 15 minutes: each input contains the preceding 24 observations, with consecutive input-to-input and last-input-to-target intervals of exactly 15 minutes. Adjacent windows on opposite sides of a period boundary may share already observed input rows, as in rolling forecasting, but every forecast target belongs to exactly one period. No Q1, Q2, or Q3--Q4 label enters the 2019 fit; no Q2 or Q3--Q4 label enters Q1 model selection; and no Q3--Q4 label enters fixed Q2 calibration. Past-only rolling calibration is evaluated separately: it can use Q3--Q4 outcomes revealed strictly before the current forecast and adds the current outcome only after issuing that forecast. Random sampling is confined to the 2019 fitting pool and to algorithmic landmark seeds; it does not create the calendar partitions.}

{\color{blue}The study uses two common meteorological input tracks across all six sites. The formal validation-selected comparison uses four wind speeds, temperature, atmospheric pressure, relative humidity, and sine/cosine encodings of four wind directions at each of the 24 strictly preceding observations, giving 15 variables per step and 360 flattened inputs. The fixed-setting sensitivity analyses retain the earlier track of four wind speeds, temperature, and the same eight directional encodings, giving 13 variables per step and 312 flattened inputs. Neither track uses past power or future meteorological values. Times written as 24:00 are normalized to the next day; all rows sharing an ambiguous duplicate timestamp are removed before chronological sorting. Missing codes ($-99$), nonfinite values, all-zero meteorological records, negative wind speeds, and directions outside $[0,360]$ are treated as missing covariates. Targets with missing power, hub wind, or temperature and windows with non-15-minute gaps are excluded by fixed rules. Other power values, including negative or above-capacity observations, are retained. Missing input values are replaced by lag-specific fitting means; an entirely missing coordinate uses zero. Feature standardization and capacity-normalized label standardization use only the observations actually fitted in that branch, excluding unused target labels in scarcity experiments. No future-value filling, clipping, or error-based exclusions are applied. The original files are preserved, although their upstream measurement and processing history is not fully documented.}

{\color{blue}Domain thresholds use valid meteorological observations from 2019 only. Farm~6 thresholds are 15.43\,m/s for wind and 10.24/31.36\,$^\circ$C for temperature; its training set contains 32,832 source and 2,076 target windows. Table~6 reports all six sites. Test membership is determined retrospectively from observed target-time weather; this protocol does not forecast event onset. The time split, missing-value rules, and common-setting comparison grids were specified before those fits. This is a temporal holdout within a previously studied public dataset.}
\end{quote}
